The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy nuclear recoil detectors, supplanting current technqiues, and we analyze potential applications and challenges associated with various types of color center-based detectors, evaluating their feasibility based on existing experimental limits with an emphasis on ongoing and near-future experiments.

Colloids interact dynamically with their surroundings through velocity changes, layer formation, and division into distinct areas. Several factors such as concentration gradients and surface affinities influence colloid movement and organization. This research investigates the behavior of dynamic colloids within varying activity gradients, where a theoretical model divides the system into zones of different activity levels. As a result, multiple stable patterns emerge, determined by the interaction between colloid concentration and surface interactions. The model's predictions can be applied to different types of interacting colloids and experimentally validated through observations of Levy flights in a medium with a time-varying diffusion rate.

This article investigates the edge spectral properties of a two-dimensional fractional quantum Hall system influenced by a magnetic field. At its charge-neutral phase, a notable feature, known as magnetoroton, emerges in the spectral behavior and is composed of two distinct particles with opposite fractional charges. The absence of spectral gaps in the system's energy spectrum leads to the emergence of numerous magnetrotons as excitations with finite energies. Our research demonstrates that particle-hole transformations among these excitations are associated with total charge regulations in the system. Furthermore, we identify additional spectral regulations involving a specific edge excitation, known as a Corbini-Greenblum mode, which occurs under two distinct conditions: the absence of magnetrotons and a total charge regulation of zero, as well as a total spin regulation of zero.

A novel approach grounded in graph theory has emerged to understand the spread of infectious diseases across interconnected populations. This method views a population divided into distinct subgroups where individuals within each subgroup intermingle freely but are isolated from others. A disease spreads dynamically on a network consisting of varying subgroups in close relation to each other. A novel nonparametric method rooted in geometry aims to automatically categorize this population into distinct subgroups based on shared transmission patterns. This is achieved through a localized clustering technique applied to probability distributions representing different subgroups and embedded in a geometry that naturally reflects their relationships, ensuring all points correspond to probability distributions of infectious disease models. A numerical simulation illustrating this methodology is provided.

Researchers utilizing the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) have successfully detected "x"-shaped anomalies in polarization patterns, often interpreted as indicative of the presence of cosmic strings. There is, however, an urgent need to verify whether these anomalies could be the result of a more plausible foreground influence. To address this concern, a computer simulation was employed to model the interference pattern created by a foreground with an "x"-shaped shape, which was then used to develop a template-based detection method to identify similar patterns in real data. The results of this simulation revealed that the most effective approach to detecting "x"-shaped patterns is to use maximum likelihood estimation, particularly through the analysis of two orthogonal polarization components. When comparing the effectiveness of circular and square templates, it became evident that the presence of discrete irregularities in the foreground can be more easily detected using a square template. Furthermore, it was found that the presence of noise can be distinguished from the pattern created by a foreground gradient at a signal-to-noise ratio of 1. Consistently with these findings, estimates of the sensitivity required to detect "x"-shaped patterns at a 95% confidence level reveal that the presence of such patterns in real data could be a result of either a cosmic string or a foreground influence, with estimated upper bounds ranging from 2% to 20% difference in distortion scale parameter ($10^{-30}$) for polarized noise levels of 10$\sigma$ and 1$\sigma$ respectively.

Our focus in this work is on reinforcement learning agents that can interpret natural language instructions and achieve goals in a given environment. It's known that natural language contains ambiguous references, especially when multiple objects are present. As a result, agents face a challenge known as referential uncertainty, which hinders their ability to effectively utilize provided object labels in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. To overcome this issue, our approach relies on the idea that a multi-object attention mechanism, combined with attention-based label filtering, can help agents efficiently respond to ambiguous labels. We achieve this by incorporating two simple modifications into the typical goal-conditioned reinforcement learning setup: introducing a filter that eliminates unnecessary label options and a multi-object attention system that focuses on relevant objects. Experimental findings on the MP3 data set demonstrate that our proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the standard baseline by 25%, and also compare favorably to a more advanced method that employs multi-step inference.

Quantum channel tomography involves determining a channel by measuring various quantum state projections. Typically, determining each element of a channel matrix requires numerous experiments. We examine the process of estimating specific channel matrix elements using shadow methods, which use linear functions to calculate expectations of the channel operator. Certain channel matrix elements can be estimated directly by evaluating the shadow operator, whereas others require probing specific input states. We explore the conditions that enable minimal experiments required to determine all channel matrix elements. We also compare shadow method channel tomography with optimal probing, analyzing how noise impacts its accuracy in both cases.

This research presents a collection of inequalities involving the Cheeger parameter, specifically for shapes bounded by convex curves within the plane. In particular, we derive sharp inequalities for shapes with polygons as boundaries, involving their perimeters, areas, and Cheeger parameters. Additionally, we derive related inequalities for shapes with smooth, convex boundaries, involving their perimeters, areas, Cheeger parameters, and inradii. These inequalities are verified through integral identity transformations and refined using the rearrangement inequality and its converse.

We investigate the joint optimization of the trajectory of a UAV and the scheduling of tasks on its onboard processors to minimize energy consumption while complying with time constraints. The path planning problem is solved using a dynamic programming approach, and a scheduling algorithm is developed to take into account the dependence between tasks and the varying computational capacities of the available processors. The effectiveness of the proposed method is illustrated through simulations considering various field-of-view parameters and the impact of noisy data on the optimal solution is also examined.

In multilayer graphene, particularly in the bilayer form, the interaction between electrons plays a crucial role. When a constant electric field is applied to this material, charge layers within each layer and across different layers move in tandem, creating multiple oscillating modes. By considering the coupling between these oscillations, researchers found that small changes can lead to instability in the material's behavior. Using a renormalization group approach, these interactions can be analyzed in detail. Focusing on the two dominant oscillatory modes in charge distribution within bilayer graphene, researchers have developed a model that accounts for the material's response to external electric fields by coupling these modes. This approach has helped establish an instability criterion, with the result that the material becomes unstable when a specific condition related to Coulomb coupling and field strength is met. This model can be applied to a variety of scenarios in bilayer graphene, giving a general framework for its behavior. Finally, researchers have explored the effects of fluctuations in the interaction between electrons on this instability, finding that the effect holds true regardless of the level of interaction between charge layers. This approach provides a framework for understanding the material's electronic response in different configurations and interacting regimes.

In this investigation, the C$_{80}$(fullerene)@Sc$_2$TbN compound has been examined for changes in conformational structure when exposed to temperatures ranging from 90 K to room temperature when adsorbed onto a nickel boron surface. Utilizing scanning tunneling microscopy, the initial configuration at 90 K displayed a structure resembling a hexahedral capsule, whereas subsequent heating to 300 K led to the transformation into a truncated tetrahedral shape observed in the bulk phase. Notably, the intermolecular distance between adsorbed molecules at room temperature was found to be 7.0 nanometers, suggesting weak van der Waals interactions between molecules. Moreover, atomic-scale imaging revealed a single molecule's intramolecular vibration frequency of 0.43 Reciprocal Angstroms, thereby providing direct evidence for its structural dynamics and thermal energy behavior.

The internet of things encompasses various devices, ranging from energy-efficient devices such as sensors and actuators to equipment with limited storage capabilities and displays. The majority of existing lightweight cryptographic algorithms employ simple operations, but still require significant processing power, storage capacity, or both. Consequently, applications such as smart meters, biomedical devices, and display-less devices struggle to implement these cryptographic solutions. To resolve this issue, we present a novel lightweight cryptographic system that addresses the energy consumption, storage constraints, and efficiency requirements of IoT devices. To evaluate the performance of the proposed solution, we conducted an energy consumption analysis using FPGAs and compared our approach with existing lightweight cryptographic algorithms based on Hamming X-10, X-16, and X-24 codes. The results indicate that our proposed method outperforms these existing solutions in terms of energy efficiency, storage efficiency, and overall efficiency.

The Ramsey series experiment measures the frequency instability of ion traps using a diverse range of sampling frequencies. This study creates a comprehensive model for ion dynamics, ion leakage, and frequency detuning, and develops a Bayesian trial design framework to optimize sampling frequencies for minimal uncertainty in estimating the stable frequency range. By employing this adaptive design approach, the study demonstrates a substantial improvement in experimental efficiency, reducing the number of sampling frequencies needed by nearly 80% compared to a traditional optimised design. Furthermore, the study's framework allows for flexible modifications to the model, for instance, by taking into account varying ion lifetimes at different sampling frequencies. This research provides a crucial framework for optimizing Ramsey series measurements, offering insights into optimizing other ion trapping measurements as well.

A new measure of node importance in graphs, called Gromov importance, is proposed, which prioritizes connections that preserve the shortest path tree topology despite local distance alterations. This importance is calculated using a central ingredient – the triangle inequality surplus – which quantifies the minimum cost of the shortest path tree. By considering the triangle inequality surplus of unimportant nodes, Gromov importance differs from other importance schemes that focus on peripheral nodes. In networks where important nodes have significant shortest path contributions, Gromov importance and betweenness centrality are closely related. In contrast, Gromov importance and other importance measures are distinct when target nodes have important shortest path contributions, which is demonstrated in sample examples. Furthermore, a multi-layer extension of Gromov importance is proposed for multi-layer graphs, which is shown to be linearly correlated with its single-layer counterpart, thus preserving key characteristics.

The Azimuthally Uniform Theory of Gravity offers an alternative to conventional gravity, postulating that every mass area acts as a uniform gravitational source that radiates energy downwards. As a result, the space surrounding massive objects is evenly filled with gravitational quanta, functionally analogous to a beam of gravity emanating from the massive objects' equators. Based on this premise, the theory derives the Poisson equation and Newton's law of gravitational attraction, replacing the conventional concept of a curved space geometry with a scenario where gravity quanta propel test particles towards a common lower elevation. This account also presents a new derivation of Newton's rotation curve, indicates that gravity is isophoric, and reveals the relationship between the gravitational constant G and Planck's constant h, as well as the speed of light c in the context of this theory.

We define three fundamental matrix operations: submixture, supermixture, and blend, representing different forms of combination. These operations establish relationships between families of matrix pencils that are equivalent in terms of size, arrangement, and scaling. For instance, submixture and supermixture correspond to operations of addition and subtraction, while blend represents an averaging process. The notion of blend operations is found to be equivalent to the definition provided by K. Dzelainis and J. A. G. Maartens in 1982. The direct and inverse approaches to matrix pencils are found to be representable through submixture, supermixture, or blend operations applied to the direct critical set. The notion of the indirect critical set can be defined as a closure of the submixture or supermixture operations related to the direct critical set. The matrix pencils belonging to a given family can be determined through a maximum or minimum representation using a specific set of operations applied to the indirect critical set. The submixture, supermixture, or blend operations enable the determination of the matrix pencils belonging to a given family and their equivalence classes. The equivalence classes can be defined as a closure of the matrix pencils belonging to a given family under the submixture, supermixture, or blend operations. The matrix pencils can be directly or indirectly critical in relation to the equivalence classes. The submixture, supermixture, or blend operations preserve certain fundamental properties of critical points. The Heron

A traditional T-duality principle in string theory applies to torus configurations but falls short when faced with twisted torus geometries. Our research develops a geometric T-duality framework capable of handling both standard and twisted torus geometies through the introduction of orthogonal bundles. This approach provides orthogonal bundles corresponding to the dual geometries of the original, and we formulate T-duality equations to describe corresponding Lagrangians. To demonstrate its applicability, we apply this theory to T-duality transformations involving twisted torus examples with SU(2) gauge fields. This work lays the foundation for a geometric T-duality theory that can treat torus geometies of any dimension by considering fiber bundles.

In graph theory, the concept of parameterized complexity involves analyzing problems that have multiple related parameters. For a specific parameter, we can examine how its value affects the problem's complexity and its various aspects. The concept of treewidth is crucial in this context, allowing us for efficient algorithmic solutions when the treewidth is reasonably limited. Building upon this concept, we can investigate graph problems while fixing the treewidth, giving rise to parameterized complexity. The present study focuses on the problem of computing shortest path distances between all pairs of vertices in planar and minor-free graphs when the treewidth is limited. The graph model includes the well-known metric tree problem, which has significant applications, including in distributed algorithms and the tractable fragments of the fixed parameter tractible (FPT) domain. For the sake of the model's simplicity, we consider the reduced treewidth, where we exclude the vertices forming the outer boundary of the treewidth tree. The obtained results show that the problem is solvable in FPT time when restricting the output size and considering the limited treewidth as a parameter. The study also proves that the problem is only weakly treewidth-approximable, confirming its inherent intractability when the treewidth is not a parameter. The proof of this result relies on a new structural graph property called the path-extended tree, which might be valuable in the future research. The provided algorithmic solution is likely to be generally applicable to the treewidth-approximable problems.

This paper examines global behavior of a type of mathematical model known as discrete-time monotonic systems. These systems have a large, smooth nonlinear part, along with a smaller, linear part. They are called discrete-time monotonic systems because they follow specific rules that ensure certain patterns in their behavior. The study focuses on systems that act in a particular way by either increasing or decreasing certain values in a system. It shows that such systems typically exhibit unique, long-term patterns of behavior, which can be either stable or unpredictable. The study also finds that in systems that act in a particular way, these patterns of behavior are consistent with each other. The results presented in this paper rely on an earlier finding that showed that discrete-time monotonic systems that act in a particular way often have unique, long-term patterns of behavior. The study shows that such systems typically exhibit stable patterns of behavior.

A new method is presented that adapts the size of a variational quantum eigensolver based on its own error, utilizing a random in-phase qubit excitation to calculate wave functions and principal norms of Fesenko operators in each iteration. This approach is suitable for near-term computers as it eliminates the need for an additional qubit to store wave functions. It has been tested on two specific problems - the Lipid A dimer molecule with only a single basis set reduction and the transverse Ising model on a specific random graph. Results show that the proposed algorithm is efficient and robust, reaching high convergence rates and performing well in diverse scenarios.

The Profound Network, a type of autoencoder, is capable of generating meaningful representations by learning a low-dimensional space where similar inputs are close to each other. However, interpreting these representations can be difficult. In this work, we suggest that probabilistic models, like the Profound Network, are inherently exploratory and can be understood as a tool for discovering new modes in a space. We reinterpreted the Profound Network's classifier as a way to identify and differentiate between similar inputs and experimented with replacing it with an alternative method, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) approximator. We designed a simplified version of the Profound Network, which we called SlimProfound, to reduce the computational cost of the classifier. Our experiments showed that SlimProfound-MAP consistently produced more accurate classifications than the standard Profound Network classifier, especially for complex inputs. Additionally, we utilized SlimProfound to develop a novel method for data compression based on model caching, which achieved superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

A cosmological framework rooted in inflation necessitates that cosmic defects become apparent in the universe's early stages. As these flaws cause distortions in the cosmic microwave background, they are, by necessity, embedded in the gravitational wave background produced by the inflationary process. The latter wave pattern is characterized by highly correlated temporal and spatial fluctuations, and detection of these features by LISA could potentially reveal the effects of cosmic defects distorting the background's spectrum. This could be interpreted as an increase in the gravitational wave amplitude while simultaneously narrowing its frequency band. It is shown that for certain models, the amplitude of the distorted background can significantly exceed expectations, potentially up to 100 times larger, with the characteristic frequency spanning between mHz and Hz. This could lead to a significant alignment of the gravitational wave background with constraints from models of primordial non-Gaussianity and accuracy cosmology, suggesting the inflationary wave pattern could be observable by LISA within reach of current astrophysical gravitational wave events detected by NANOGrav, Advanced LIGO-Virgo and future cosmological surveys to probe the acceleration of the universe.

A comprehensive study of the coma of Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) has been conducted using data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's Atacama Compact Array. This comet's proximity to perihelion in March 2017 made it an ideal target for observation, and research focused on the molecular composition, spatial distribution of emissions, and gas and dust environments near its surface and outer regions. Ionized gas, H2O, H2CO, CO, and CS emissions were detected, and analysis revealed a diverse gas distribution comprising of water, methanol, and cyano groups, as well as a complex organic environment. Comparisons with other cometary studies provided an opportunity to analyze spectral variations, and findings suggest that CO and CS emissions originate from farther away from the comet's nucleus. This could be an indication of sublimation occurring in areas where water and organic compounds coexist to form CS. Alternatively, it may also point to the presence of carbon and sulfur-containing organic molecules that have not yet been extensively studied in cometary research.

We introduce an uncomplicated method for producing speech without labels by utilizing existing speech datasets. Our approach leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) to learn the target distribution of speech, relying on publicly available speech embeddings derived from datasets like LibriSpeech. This technique has several benefits, as it bypasses complex sequence-to-segment generation methods, eliminates the need for aligned pairs of speech and text, and facilitates flexible waveforms generation via a posterior GAN. Our results show that a straightforward GAN performs better in human evaluations compared to more advanced generative models, such as WaveNet and Transformer, and even surpasses unsupervised speech synthesis based on extensive, manually annotated data pairs.

In this research, a relationship between the Tsallis holographic dark energy radius and density is established using the Lagrangian method. A negative pressure calculation is then carried out, and the model's behavior is analyzed through parameters a and q. The study demonstrates that by increasing parameters a and q, the model's dark energy fraction rises, displaying a parameter-dependent behavior. A theorem confirming that the energy density of this model tends towards zero as the radius diminishes is also presented. In addition, the study investigates the model's thermodynamic stability by examining its heat capacity and finds that it satisfies the Gibbs-Duhem equation, as well as its relation with the equation of state parameter. A comparison with the quintessence model completes the study.

Multi-objective optimization problems that are non-linear and mixed can be difficult to solve, especially when including integers. Many hybrid algorithms have been created in response to this difficulty, but one approach that offers a guaranteed solution is model-based multi-objective branch and bound algorithms. Model-based algorithms have the advantage of only considering feasible solutions, which can significantly reduce computation time. This paper proposes a new branch and bound algorithm that utilizes a nonlinear programming solver, specifically Nonlinear Programming using the SLSQP method, to find multi-objective solutions. This approach proposes the use of a promising combination, evaluating and sorting solutions based on the Euclidean distance to the ideal point using the two-dimensions of the hypervolume indicator and the minimum distance to the Pareto-front, which outperformed previous models. This new algorithm was tested on a set of known difficult optimization problems and demonstrated the ability to find high-quality solutions that approximate the true Pareto-front.

The concept of linked Lie groupoids corresponds to a specific category of differential groupoids that exhibit connectedness and matching nearby movement characteristics. Similar to how abelian groups fit within the broader framework of rings, we establish that connected and matchable whole Lie groupoids form a natural subset of the class of all local Lie groupoids. Additionally, any whole connected matchable Lie groupoid meets the criteria to be a central Lie subgroupoid within any host Lie groupoid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the construction of a whole connected matchable Lie groupoid from a given local one is feasible and dependent on a specific choice of whole real number per connected component.

In recent years, the exponential growth in biomedical data has led to a pressing need for standardized data sharing practices, while also creating challenges for sharing vast amounts of complex data. To address these issues, researchers have been embracing cyberinfrastructure tools, notably data portals that cater to specific biomedical fields. These portals enhance data exchange and management, while their number poses a challenge for researchers in identifying the most suitable one for their needs. To streamline the process, researchers can consult comprehensive portals that index and facilitate access to multiple specialized portals, thereby accelerating and safely managing data exchange.

Aspect-based emotion analysis focuses on identifying the emotions expressed towards specific aspects in a given sentence. This task is crucial for grasping how people emotionally react to products, services, and individuals. Current approaches have made notable progress but still struggle to capture the underlying sentiment orientation - whether the expressed emotions have a positive or negative connotation. This task is complex due to the scarcity of relevant data and the challenge of capturing subtle sentiment information. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a new approach called Guided Contrastive Pre-Training (GCT), which leverages large amounts of readily available data from the general domain to aid in learning sentiment. By leveraging dual contrastive learning techniques, this method enhances the model's ability to distinguish between the target aspect and other irrelevant entities. To further improve performance, this approach combines positive and negative guidance to help the model discern the specific emotion and its underlying sentiment. Experiments on the SemEval 2018 tasks 2 and 3 demonstrate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.

When investigating the relationship between an exposure and an outcome using data from cases and controls, it is crucial to assess whether the effect appears larger than expected due to bias and confounding effects. This is particularly important because traditional measures of association, such as odds ratios (ORs), might not accurately represent the size of the bias and confounding effects. In contrast, mediation effects appear to be particularly vulnerable to bias, and there is a noticeable absence of studies examining mediation effects in case-control studies despite existing methods for assessing bias and confounding effects. This article aims to introduce novel methods for evaluating mediation effects in case-control studies, particularly with binary mediators and exposures. These methods provide ranges with confidence intervals that account for bias and confounding effects, and they are exemplified using data from a study on the association between intrapartum HIV prevention and risk of HIV transmission to infants.

This research delves into the secure communication networks for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) to enhance resilience against failures. To achieve this, we develop a comprehensive approach to designing the RIS phase matrix and source covariance matrix. These matrices are designed to maximize the minimum secrecy rate under equipment constraints. Initially, we formulate the problem as a non-convex optimization issue and use the block coordinate descent framework to create a feasible solution. This framework splits the optimization problem into two sub-problems and uses alternating minimization. The first subproblem involves optimizing the RIS phase matrix through a new reformulation that transforms it into a convex problem using the Khatri-Rao product. The second subproblem aims to maximize the lower bound of the secrecy rate of the secondary user. By iteratively applying these two sub-problems, we obtain a feasible solution that approaches an optimal solution as equilibrating the two matrices. Our simulation results confirm the efficacy of this design method in achieving a high and stable secrecy rate for both primary and secondary users despite RIS failure.

To rectify biases hampering machine learning system fairness, a straightforward strategy involves rethinking approach values. Yet, approaching this challenge for complex systems like financial portfolios proves challenging due to the inherent complexity of outcomes and parameters. Resampling and renaming methods aim to mitigate bias by leveraging diverse outcomes and parameter values, but their efficacy for complex systems remains unclear. We developed an evaluation framework for evaluating fairness in outcome approachability by applying it to a large portfolio's management. Our strategy, named Executive Function, compares each offshoot with a summary of the system's potential outcomes, but instead of using forecasts, we look back at what's happened. We found that managing a portfolio this way can be beneficial, especially when faced with uncertainty, and that diversifying outcomes and parameter values can lead to better performance. However, this benefit only arises when we consider past values for asset development, and not when we think about what might happen in the future. Moreover, our tests show that simply changing the names of values, rather than truly altering them, does not lead to better fairness.

The topological structure of noncommutative principal countable bundles within the realm of C*-algebras can be described through a two-part process, where first, a corresponding G-C*-algebra is identified by establishing a universal action of a discrete or discrete-like group G on a C*-algebra A. This results in a noncommutative principal countable bundle whose base space is the space of all universal actions, with fiber being the G-algebraic quotient [A,G]. Secondly, a corresponding G-action on a C*-dynamical system (B,H,U) can be found, leading to another noncommutative principal countable bundle with base space [A,G] and fiber B. The collection of these structures forms a natural association between universal actions and corresponding dynamical systems. This correspondence encompasses both commutative and noncommutative topological structures, where specific instances manifest when considering G-action's that induce finitely many isomorphisms within the corresponding quotient maps. Examples of noncommutative principal countable bundles have been found in relation to free unitary G-action's on AF C*-algebras.

Moreover, we define a new cardinal invariant, denoted $\mathfrak{u}\kappa$, which represents the least cardinality of sets whose union with any other such set has a strict $\kappa$-intersection, and prove that $\mathfrak{u}\kappa$ effectively captures the essence of $\kappa$-ultrafilter addition in a more general framework.

A quantum double-group model extending the IOPScissors model of Euler-Pauli-Goudsmit is developed to describe R-parity violating states in superheavy nuclei. The new state in the model corresponds to a spheroidal vibration of the double-rotor, assumed to be a member of the 1^+ multiplet, along with a negative-energy state of the double-rotor, belonging to the 1^+ multiplet. This new state is predicted to have a weakly R-parity-invariant characteristic, with a substantial admixture of the double-rotor's negative-energy state, resulting in a local minimum in the energy dispersion relation. This scenario bears similarities to a scenario of quantum scissor modes coupling in even-even nuclei, produced by the orbital crossing of two rotors, with the described phenomenon potentially observed in superheavy nuclei with the required mix of the double-rotor's positive and negative energy states.

A novel numerical approach is presented for solving first-order nonlinear hyperbolic PDEs and conjugate gradient methods for more general elliptic PDEs. This method employs cell-mean values to approximate the fluxes required for the hyperbolic PDEs, which also serves as a suitable solver for linear elliptic PDEs. To demonstrate its performance, the proposed approach is initially evaluated on the Burgers equation, which reveals exceptional accuracy at a low computational cost with a range of high-order neural network architectures. Furthermore, the proposed method is adapted to solve the Poisson equation, an important linear elliptic PDE, and is also extended to handle the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, a second-order nonlinear hyperbolic PDE.

The ALICE Collaboration delves into enhancing the LHCb and future LHC experiments, exceeding expectations beyond Run 3. In this paper, we explore multiple avenues for upgrade initiatives, going beyond what's anticipated for Run 3. We will examine potential improvements in particle identification, investigating the feasibility of introducing a high-energy muon spectrometer above the existing detector. This novel concept would offer several advantages: (a) increased acceptance for heavy flavor hadron decay products including muons, enhancing flavor identification and offering better competition to LHCb; (b) improved precision on high-energy muons from charm baryon decays, aiding in better understanding these particles; (c) enhanced capabilities for photon and neutral meson identification through the study of their decays into internal muon colliders; (d) increased scope for beyond the Standard Model physics, such as searching for anomalies in the dimuon mass spectrum consistent with an excess of an invisible afferent signature at CDF. Supplementing the proposed detector concept with a detailed cost breakdown and scheduling plan will also be presented.

We've discovered that the entanglement between the quantum vacuum states defined by different time zones exhibits a geometric phase delay, stemming from the temporal Uhruheffect. Building on this finding, we suggest an experimental approach to detect this effect by observing the interference between two possible paths of a quantum particle. In the context of Inflation, our proposal implies that, as seen by a freely falling observer, even the causal relationship between past and future events becomes ambiguous and dependent on the geometric relationship between these events.

Researchers investigate a phenomenon where a differential operator's global symbol corresponds to a vector bundle and corresponds to a specific geometric structure. They call this occurrence a characteristic structure, defined by the operator's global principal symbol, that satisfies certain conditions. Characteristic structures exhibit the classifying space's positivity properties and significant structural features. The study of these structures is highly sought-after due to their broad implications in geometric and conformal geometry. Researchers have developed new methods for constructing characteristic structures, including examples within Riemann surface geometry and pseudo-Riemann surface geometry. They have also made significant progress in understanding the relationship between these structures and the classifying space. Specifically, they have shown that certain characteristic structures corresponding to second-order differential operators are positive and have non-trivial groupings. Some of these results have far-reaching implications in understanding the geometry of specific spaces, such as hyperbolic surfaces and Gelfand-Shawlike surfaces.

Within non-abelian gauge theories, a subclass of Chern-Simons terms can be accommodated, potentially mimicking the properties of an non-abelian aether-like term. Due to their non-topological nature, these terms don't restrict gauge invariance; however, their physical implications are still governned by the background symmetry of the system. A study on non-abelian aether-like terms reveals their relationship with chiral anomalies and their manifestation in the equations of motion at finite temperature. Additionally, the study illustrates the counterterm principle in non-abelian aether-like terms at finite temperature.

This study introduces an innovative information extraction framework known as CUSE, which leverages the collective knowledge of the entire research community to inform analysis and annotation. By combining results from a simple and straightforward crowdsourcing campaign with sophisticated machine learning algorithms, CUSE accurately identifies the universal subject-verb-object and entity-related object relationships within academic papers. When compared to state-of-the-art syntactic analyzers, CUSE exhibits superior performance on crowdsourced data and when trained on existing annotated datasets, outperforms these analyzers while also detecting additional entity-related object relationships. CUSE achieves significant gains in performance over existing natural language processing tools and is made available through an integrated web platform allowing for seamless information extraction.

The study of neutron star and black hole mergers, including their aftermath, offers valuable insights into the early universe. To better comprehend these events, we simulated the scenario where a neutron star undergoes a merger with a neutron star or a black hole, and we focus on the immediate aftermath. A powerful neutrino flux emerges from an accretion disk surrounding the remnant, discharging energy and lepton number while driving mass loss. The disk's magnetic field grows due to dynamo and turbulence, and we found that about 15% of the mass loss is carried away by particles, with the rest going down the black hole. We calculated the potential postmerger electromagnetic outbursts and compared them to observations from short gamma-ray burst sources, and found some discrepancies. Then, we used our simulations to determine the impact on the neutron star's magnetic field, and found that a certain fraction of the mass loss carries magnetic flux, resulting in a net gain for the remnant. This is due to the difference in conductivity between the disk and the star, and we found that a typical increase in magnetic field corresponds to a 30% enhancement, and this effect could partially explain magnetic fields observed in millisecond pulsars.

We employed data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program to analyze and classify 1300 dwarf elliptical galaxies, some of which exhibited significantly larger masses than predicted by established theoretical models. To understand this phenomenon, we developed an analytical framework incorporating the relative importance of accretion and mergers in building up massive galaxies. Factors like the rate of large merger events, the density of galaxies in a given area, and the characteristics of galaxy mass distribution all play crucial roles. Inverting this model, also known as recovering the merger tree, revealed key information regarding local galaxy density, the occurrence rate of mergers, and the characteristics of galaxies being merged. Notably, our findings suggest that large mergers are significantly more common than previously thought and are the primary means by which massive galaxies form. Moreover, our research indicates that galaxies with higher mass have seen the greatest significant increase in merger rates.

This paper offers a detailed explanation of a model initially described in a previous study, the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation. According to this model, gravitational force acts as a repulsive effect under certain conditions of velocity and direction in an orbit, outside the range of a central mass's normal attractive influence. A scenario illustrating this phenomenon is provided in the form of a simulation. Furthermore, the study examines various ejections resulting from this repulsive force and suggests that this effect could be the cause of bipolar ejections, a phenomenon that has been observed in star systems.

The origin of fast radio bursts remains largely unknown, largely due to the lack of detailed observations of their behavior following the initial pulse. Recent discoveries of a delayed emission component in some FRBs suggest that their emission is not limited to a single event. Our research involves an in-depth analysis of seven FRBs with high signal quality that exhibit no initial pulse in their host galaxies, and an additional eight FRBs with weaker signals that also show no initial pulse in their galaxies. Our findings indicate a range of emission levels and rise times for these delayed components. The delayed components' spectra align with a power-law model with an index of -2.59 and may indicate a pattern of energy decay over time. These results significantly narrow the possible parameters for the delayed emission model, and help to identify suitable telescope observations to find more FRBs with these delayed components.

To increase the high-pulse-energy capability of laser systems, particularly those using $Q$-switching approaches, several high-power fabrication methods have been explored. This research outlines strategies for designing high-energy laser systems, focusing on optimizing crystal properties and introducing spatial-temporal light patterning abilities. The importance of choosing the correct crystal type, position, and density in high-energy applications is demonstrated. Furthermore, the development of laser systems incorporating crystalline thin films is detailed, and the ability to replicate existing high-power laser configurations using these films is shown.

The capacity for machines to create text based on visual input has significant implications for multiple sectors, including commerce, tourism, and customer service. Current methods, which rely on task-specific designs, are limited in their ability to generalize and apply to unseen domains. To address this issue, we propose a transfer learning strategy that allows pre-trained language models to leverage image data for improved text generation. Our approach involves retraining a language model to take image features into consideration when creating high-quality text, and demonstrates this through the case study of creating English tour descriptions.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports private Monero transactions. The modified protocol is designed for the Global Equity Association, utilizing Delegated Proof of Stake and RingCT for enhanced security and transparency. However, our primary focus is on the enhanced RingCT protocol, aiming to increase off-chain transaction efficiency while maintaining anonymity through the use of DLSN leases. By combining leased DLSNs with a binary tree encoding method, we achieve faster and more efficient transactions that can be processed quicker by clients. This approach allows for faster DLSN renewal and reduced transaction sizes, resulting in lower costs and faster processing speeds.

We've developed a method known as Brightness Scans, which is used to construct high-precision beam profiles at the ILC collision point by recording extremely low-intensity signals from highly dispersed bunches. The technique is versatile and can be applied across bunch integration techniques, whether using single-bunch scanning or scanning independent bunch slices. We've tested this method in laboratory settings, probing signals with known levels of radiation, and compared the results to simulate the data, also providing theoretical background explanations.

In the medical field, studies frequently rely on continuous measurement variables, which are typically analyzed using straightforward parametric models.  However, in clinical research, it's not always feasible or cost-effective to collect extensive measurements from every participant.  As a result, statistical models often rely on a limited dataset, posing significant challenges.  This paper explores various strategies for addressing these issues, which we denote as "informing" a parametric model model.  We examine multiple approaches, such as kernel smoothing, spline-based models, and neural networks, which we test on simulated and real-world data from a genetic study, focusing on patients with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.  Our analysis involves leveraging information from a related condition, hyperactivity disorder, to better understand the characteristics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.  We developed methods to inform our models through low-dimensional representations of related conditions, which we tested on multiple metrics.  Our findings indicate that taking into account the characteristics of a related condition can enhance our understanding of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

Our analysis of the decays $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(10828)\pi^+\pi^-$ and $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(10668)π^+\pi^-$ suggests that these two pis are not a typical back-to-back pair. Since the Upsilon(10668) and Upsilon(10828) have broad lines and their masses overlap, a direct comparison of their mass spectra is not feasible. However, by assuming that Upsilon(10668) and Upsilon(10828) are Lorentz- invariant pairs, we can study their spin structures and interpret the Upsilon(10753) decay widths through the Upsilon(10668, 10828) pi^+ pi^- channel. This analysis indicates Upsilon(10753) decay widths of 44 keV and 114 keV with Upsilon(10668) and Upsilon(10828) respectively. Additionally, our findings reveal that Upsilon(10753) decays at a rate of around 270 eV into Upsilon(11020) particles, and show that Upsilon(10753) has a spin-parity of 3d, with a significant anomalous decay width in comparison to Uppsilon(11020) pi.

We introduce a novel optimization technique, AskewSGD, specifically designed to efficiently train deep neural networks utilizing quantization. By incorporating range-constrained optimization, our method allows us to train such networks with a larger step size than previously possible, thereby mitigating accuracy degradation caused by aggressive quantization. AskewSGD leverages range extension, precision increase, and stochastic approaches to ensure precise results. Our method outperforms existing solutions, requiring significantly larger batch sizes, reducing computational costs and memory requirements. AskewSGD's effectiveness is demonstrated on various models and quantization strategies for image classification tasks, achieving comparable results to floating-point baselines.

Over the past few decades, there has been a significant shift in the study of robots, with many moving away from traditional rigid designs. This shift is towards innovative robots characterized by softness, flexibility, and adaptability. These robots are expected to excel in various areas, such as healthcare, where they can safely interact with humans. Given their unique nature, standard robot planning and control methods require substantial modifications. This article offers a comprehensive overview of the methods used in soft robot control, focusing on their applications, limitations, and future challenges. The techniques discussed are model driven control methods, which incorporate specific strategies based on the type of model used - ranging from theoretical to simulated to sensory data. The analysis includes notable research in this field, evaluates their effectiveness, and identifies the key obstacles that need to be addressed. Moreover, this work aims to provide valuable insights for scientists and engineers working in this field to pinpoint their current level of expertise and the areas that need attention. Finally, this study offers expert opinions on the current state of the art to facilitate the identification of the most critical challenges that need to be overcome.

This article re-examines the Jacobi group ((E_6(R) varg) and its subgroups from an arithmetic perspective, focusing specifically on the unramified case. As a result, we derive expressions for the associated Hecke rings and their bases, as well as computational formulas for the automorphic forms generated by the Jacobi group. Notably, our evaluation of the Jacobi forms and their associated Hecke rings aligns with the findings of Kac, Tamiya, and Kozima. We build upon their work, providing explicit expressions that had been missing from their research. Our approach combines elements from the principles of Gelfand-Fuks resolution and Kostant root system analysis. This method yields an alternative representation of the Jacobi group as a 18-dimensional even unipotent group. Furthermore, we have developed a publicly accessible C-code for the Jacobi group and its associated Hecke ring, facilitating efficient computation of Jacobi forms and their associated Hecke eigenvalues.

A newly developed generative model, hidden generative adversarial networks (HGANs), has demonstrated its ability to generate genuine data images in a target domain by learning its conditional probability distribution. In this study, the HGAN paradigm is further explored by incorporating the principles of generative adversarial inference, thereby enhancing its ability to replicate the target distribution. Two distinct methods are introduced to achieve this - the first involves the incorporation of dual adversarial components, thereby replacing the original discriminative model in the training process; the second method generates synthetic data images directly using an adversarial inference classifier. Our extensive evaluations confirm that HGANs with these modified models outperform their traditional counterparts across a range of domain adaptation tasks.

A crucial component in any stochastic simulation is the method used for sampling from an irregular probability space. Two relatively recent techniques, Hierarchical Sampling and Stratified Sampling, excel at accommodating complex probability spaces, in contrast to traditional Quasi-Monte Carlo methods. While Stratified Sampling often underperforms due to the restrictions imposed by its component sampling methods, these components can also be replaced with more sophisticated alternatives, such as Phase Functions or Adaptive classes, to enhance Stratified Sampling's efficiency and effectiveness. Our investigation compares these advanced samplers to Hierarchical Sampling, revealing them to be substantially superior in both efficiency and accuracy across a range of multivariate probability space scenarios.

In graph distance labeling, each vertex is assigned a label indicating its distance to a specific reference point; a central vertex acts as a distance label distributor. The label assignment problem aims to find the minimum number of labels required to cover a given graph. This paper introduces a new paradigm for efficiently finding shortest paths and serving as a distance label distributor in large, comprehensive graphs. Our solution leverages a novel max-plus linear system-based approach, allowing central vertex identification and shortest path finding in a single, fixed time complexity, independent of the input size, albeit with a dependence on the vertex count. Our results on real-world networks verify the substantial retrieval speed enhancements this paradigm offers over conventional methods.

Research into open quantum systems has shown the development of conserved distribution functions describing the momentum distribution and correlations of related bosonic systems. These distribution functions can be derived from the Schrödinger equation solution for a open system or by mapping the original problem into a quadratic form in an extended space. We apply this method to a modified Hubbard model, which exhibits complex many-body interactions and non-local coupling to an external bath. By representing the bath as two separate entities with opposing properties, we determine the system's distribution functions and analyze their evolution over time. These functions are further linked to the system's density matrix to study its quantum state. We study the effects of various parameters, including cubical mean-field energy and non-local bath interactions on the system's properties.
