Our proposed approach offers a comprehensive, mesh-based model for creating
virtual human avatars. This method generates a avatar from a few marked key
points on an image, yielding a realistic three-dimensional representation
that is aware of its pose. Unlike traditional models, our method achieves
high-fidelity results and trains end-to-end without the need for pre-built 3D
templates. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through live video
demostrations and showcase its ability to handle arbitrary avatar appearances
and states by employing a built-in mesh editor.

This research delves into the effect of heavily distorted images on visual understanding. Unlike images with minor irregularities, those with intense distortions, such as those with information gaps or extreme luminance fluctuations, trigger distinct visual cues and necessitate unique processing mechanisms. Studies examining human performance through both detailed photorealistic image manipulation tests and one-of-a-kind "binary mix-up" tasks reveal two key findings. Firstly, humans exhibit remarkable resilience in resisting the influence of distorted information, even in complex visual tasks. Secondly, this phenomenon is uniquely tied to human vision and cannot be easily replicated by non-human entities, regardless of their experience or sophistication. From a practical standpoint, our research raises important implications for the accurate labeling and evaluation of distorted images in machine learning applications.

We examine the finite temperature molecular expression of the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory at low temperatures, specifically focusing on a toroidal space with a banded structure. The thermal molecular transform is evaluated in terms of a finite basis set spanning the space. The resulting eigenvalues of the molecular operator reveal a connection to the Askey-Wilson algebra. The findings imply that the molecular expression can be represented by a sum of three trilinear terms over a three-parameter set. The Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind and a modified version of the Chebyshev polynomials, denoted as $U_{n(\lambda)}(k)$, are discovered to be the eigenstates of the molecular expression. The relationship between the eigenvalues and the group SL(2, $\mathbb{C}$) |k| is explored, and an inversion of the molecular expression near its minimum and maximum values for specific values of $\lambda_i$ is observed. The molecular expression is also shown to be applicable to the calculation of partition functions and knot invariants for the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory. The findings suggest that the molecular expression may have potential in studying Wess-Zumino-Witten models.

Our investigation utilizes cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations to study a 2D weakly-connected quantum spin lattice containing frustrated units of three interconnected spins. By focusing on a stabilised lattice pattern resulting from the competition between the ordering of spin clusters and neighbouring spin interactions, we studied the impact of applied strain. Findings suggest the existence of two distinct types of discrete energy transitions, one associated with the reorientation of spin clusters within the trimer units and another related to the collective movement of clusters across the lattice. Further development indicates that the stabilised cluster ordering can transform into a more long-range ordered state of trimers upon increase in applied strain. This transition can shift towards lower temperatures and is facilitated by the increased movement of trimers at strain levels where the cluster ordering begins to degrade. Ultimately, long-range ordering can be achieved at specific strain levels that favor specific lattice patterns.

Recent breakthroughs in few-shot learning for NLP have shown that large language models can be effectively modified to successfully complete a variety of tasks, all while using essentially the same code. To build on this, researchers have been trying to extend this concept to zero-shot learning across the broader spectrum of NLP tasks. To achieve this, they aim to compile a massive set of tasks, known as a dataset assemblage, and then modify a pre-trained language model to successfully complete these tasks. However, the process of selecting a suitable dataset assemblage and then adjusting the language model to successfully complete these tasks has been found to be very labor-intensive and difficult to scale. To overcome this, we've found a way to split the cost of selecting and adjusting the dataset assemblage into smaller, more manageable pieces, thus making the process easier and more efficient. By breaking down the cost, we can then use our method to create a variety of highly optimized language models, each of which is specifically tuned to complete a different dataset assemblage. To validate our method, we've assembled a collection of 46 NLP tasks, known as the ConceptAsm-Z, and then trained a series of highly optimized language models to successfully complete these tasks. Our results show that our method outperforms previous approaches by a significant margin, thus providing a powerful new tool for NLP research and application.

Recent research into the NMSSM model has centered on how it accounts for the LHC search results for an electric charge-$2/3$ fermion, the dark matter phenomenon and the effects of the electroweak phase transition on the universe's early history, which may lead to the discovery of gravitational waves. To better understand these findings, analysis was conducted within the framework of variational method and one-loop approach in the context of two different scenarios, both of which were based on the presence of specific sets of soft-SUSY-breaking parameters and included a correct $Z_3$ symmetry implementation. This analysis allowed for the determination of the locations of the critical points of the phase transition and the magnitude of the gravitational waves, which may be confirmed through the detection of the primordial universe's density fluctuations.

We introduce a new technique to identify 1.5 millimeter redshifts using broadband cross-correlations. We're employing an algorithm, High-z Sudoku, to scan through a vast parameter space and identify the most likely signals. This approach, tested on ALMA common user data, can pinpoint redshifts with 10% accuracy and detect potential signals up to z=5 with high confidence. With the advent of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's (ALMA) increased sensitivity, we predict that signals from extremely distant sources, specifically those with temperatures ranging from C to C, can be detected across a wide range of redshifts between z=5 to z=20. This powerful observational capability will allow us to identify up to 20 signals from extremely distant sources, specifically those with temperatures ranging from C to C, across the entire range of redshifts between z=5 to z=20, in the next two years.

The study of low-temperature properties in Heisenberg magnets with $S=1/2$ on the triangular lattice reveals two distinct phenomena, namely, the formation of pseudo-Voigt kink structures and continuous phase transitions, which have been previously unobserved in similar systems. The emergence of these features is closely associated with symmetry-breaking and symmetry-conserving ground states, respectively. In systems exhibiting a critical temperature-induced phase transition, the symmetry-conserving nature implies that the phase transition preserves its structural integrity; in contrast, the critical temperature-induced phase transition is characterised by a loss of structural symmetry. A detailed analysis of the two models on the triangular lattice, namely, the pyrochlore quantum spin ice and the honeycomb model, demonstrates that the former displays a lower critical dimension characterized by a ground state featuring local dipole moments that shift from discrete to liquid states upon increasing distance from the critical point, whereas the latter exhibits a higher critical dimension characterized by a continuous phase transition from the symmetric short-range ordered state to the long-wave spin liquid state upon increasing distance from the critical point.

In our study on the SU(3) - Higgs theory, we investigated the intricate balance between electromagnetic interactions and strong coupling effects on high-energy particles. By utilizing the TRIMM algorithm to continuously monitor the energy distribution of particles and adjusting the Higgs mass as a proportion of the energy, we pinpointed the moment when electromagnetic interactions are rendered ineffective at high energies. This occurred at an energy of approximately 36.5 GeV, where the Higgs mass and energy are in perfect proportion. Notably, when comparing this result to theoretical predictions, we found a notable discrepancy, with our findings deviating from these predictions by as much as 10%. This contrast highlights the significant challenge in accurately modeling electromagnetic interactions at extremely high energies. Moreover, our results demonstrated that this challenge could be overcome by employing a novel computational approach, where the momentary state of particles is continuously reassessed without interruption.

Cr$_2$Al adopts a hexagonal close-packed crystal structure and exhibits a type-$D$ antiferromagnetic arrangement below $272$ K. In this study, the magnetic arrangement is further investigated through neutron diffraction measurements, revealing an in-plane magnetic structure. Moreover, the neutron scattering intensity from above the transition temperature is consistent with type-$F$ antiferromagnetic order. Magnetization measurements under varying field orientations indicate a higher response to the field when it is applied within the plane and demonstrate a spin freezing effect below $60$ K, which is evident from ac magnetization and zero-field cooled magnetization measurements.

A previous kinetic model introduced a new collision model that took into account varying collision frequencies based on speed, in an attempt to improve models of rarefied gas flows more accurately. In this study, a new expression for the collision frequency was derived using an expression for the transport cross-section, which was derived from a potential function describing interactions between molecules. In particular, an expression for the transport cross-section was derived using an approximation for a potential function with a soft repulsive character. As a result of this new model, the new kinetic model was shown to reduce to the Maxwell model when certain conditions are met. In addition to this, the new kinetic model was compared against full dynamical simulations in two scenarios: one where molecules interact with a particular wall, and another where they interact with each other within a particular flow. In these comparisons, the new kinetic model was found to more accurately represent actual flow behaviors while the full dynamical simulation was found to have a particular flaw in its accuracy.

Building upon the concept of natural language as a source of instruction, we aim to create a neural interpreter for text that relies on external knowledge rather than relying heavily on pre-trained models. We employ the T0 architecture, which we modify to incorporate knowledge from external sources. In contrast to other approaches, we integrate the external knowledge directly into the model's decoding process using knowledge-related prompts. This method allows the model to utilize additional knowledge to generate outputs without requiring pre-training or heavily supervised data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by leveraging public sources of external knowledge to develop a neural interpreter that can access deeper understanding of text. We test the model's ability to explain and analyze concepts of separate research fields by utilizing online knowledge sources and prompts to induce the model to include field-specific terms not commonly found in text data, which are absent in our training data. Additionally, we provide the dataset and code used in this research for other scholars to replicate and build upon our findings.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will determine how quarks and gluons interact in a high-energy environment, based on advanced luminosity measurements from a cutting-edge collider. To achieve this, a sophisticated detector system will be constructed, incorporating advanced radiation-resistant materials and a complex detector design. A critical component of the detector is the silicon tracking sensor system, which has recently undergone significant development, leveraging a modular silicon architecture. This innovative approach, based on advanced technology, has enabled the production of complex components with superior characteristics, opening doors for sophisticated sensor designs. A recent workshop gathered experts from various fields to discuss global advancements in silicon sensor development, including case studies of successful prototypes and the prospects for future collaborations. This paper contributes to that discussion with a focus on EIC sensors, presenting the progress in silicon sensor development for the EIC and highlighting potential future developments.

A sudden and dramatic drop in optical brightness observed in the active galaxy M60 UC1 may be the result of a rare optical explosion, similar to those seen in TDEs, that was initially mistaken for a pulsating event due to its characteristic Poynting-Jefimenko radiative patterns. This new interpretation is supported by several features of the light curve. Firstly, it can explain a sudden drop in optical brightness using a small number of ions without relying on unfavorable interstellar medium conditions. Secondly, it matches the expected amplitude of optical fluctuations in a region with gas ions. Furthermore, it leads to a calculation of a megagaussary magnetic field, and finally, it results in a significant energy release of around 5 x 10^43 ergs per second, a magnitude consistent with that of microquasars and quiescent state black holes.

Researchers have observed significant progress in studying the external magnetic fields of stars using advanced spectropolarimetry techniques. A particular example of such progress involves the study of HD58260, whose external magnetic field is generated as a result of plasma interactions with the star's atmosphere. A high-resolution spectropolarimetric device was used to observe HD58260 over multiple occasions spanning more than a decade. The analysis of these observations has confirmed the existence of a shock heated external atmosphere with a lower boundary located at approximately 200,000 km. The average external magnetic field strength at this point is approximately 1000 Gauss. Notably, the observed magnetic field variation over a relatively short period of time, with a minimum and maximum value of around 800 and 1200 Gauss. The observed timeframes for these variations ranged from a few minutes to a week. The magnetic field oscillations appear to be associated with a specific period of 15-18 minutes. The authors attribute these magnetic field fluctuations to the movement of magnetic flux tubes, suggesting that POLIS has the potential to become a key instrument in studying the dynamic behavior of magnetic fields in stars.

A operator representation based on a free boson algebra analyzes the Dunkl operator's intertwining operator in a one-dimensional vector space. This representation utilizes the image and kernel of the Dunkl operator within the boson algebra's coherent states framework. Coherent states are employed to derive a depolarizing dust model in one dimension. Additionally, this study traces the evolution of the coherent states over time in a one-dimensional context, corresponding to a polynomial basis in a finite-dimensional Fock space. Consequently, this study offers an operator representation based on the boson algebra for resolving the Dunkl operator's differential equation in a one-dimensional space. This operator representation study serves as a one-dimensional version of a preceding study on a free fermion depiction of the Dunkl intertwining operator.

A galaxy's star formation rate can be constrained by observing its emission of specific atomic lines, which correlates with the rate of new star births. Additionally, studying a galaxy's gas composition is vital in understanding its star formation history, as it also influences the formation of new stars. Analyzing a galaxy's gas and dust properties help reveal its stellar genesis. Using a high-resolution telescope like the Atacama Large Millimeter Array, we can examine a galaxy's chemistry. Our examination of the dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, using a vast ATM observation of its H30$\alpha$ line emission, shows its star formation rate is very low and its metal content is also very low. Using this observation, we calculated a metallicity-based star formation rate that diverged from the observed rate. A proposed explanation for this difference is that highly metal-rich clouds are hidden among the overall metal-poor gas, meaning they do not affect the metallicity-based star formation rate. Using this information, we estimated the metallicity and abundance of carbon in NGC 5253, finding that it is consistent with the values from spectroscopic analysis. A comparison with another observation method confirmed that the interstellar gas of NGC 5253 has low metal content and is rich in carbon. Our examination of the H30$\alpha$ line also indicated that nitrogen abundance is very low. A proposed explanation for this is that it reflects the nitrogen abundance in NGC 5253. We demonstrate that for a virtually cyclic group G, the category of G-orbit equivalence is both extremely rigid and rigidly indistinguishable. Additionally, this corresponds to an equivalence between the sets of G-measure spaces that have non-trivial Maslov semigroups and those that are formally bound.

This study introduces a novel estimation technique for the conditional expectation function (CEF) with a mixed domain having both continuous and countable dimensions. The proposed method integrates a kernel estimator for the continuous part and a traditional nearest neighbor estimator for the discrete part. The general risk assessment is then specialized to commonly encountered discrete domains such as finite and countably infinite spaces, as well as specific examples like categorical data with an unspecified number of categories. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields consistent CEF estimates and the associated rates of convergence are also determined and quantified.

This research introduces an observer design for tracking the state of an SIS model, which involves determining the exact ratio of infected individuals to total individuals, as well as the exact fraction of susceptible individuals. The proposed observer relies on measuring the squared magnitude of the output, rather than the output itself, in order to compensate for time delays in the model. A specific expression for the measurement matrix is derived, and numerical simulations are performed to assess the observer's performance.

Recent advancements in knowledge graph learning have led to significant improvements in handling temporal data with graph structures. Connection prediction is a crucial aspect of this research, typically solved through a classification task utilizing past event information. Prior approaches in this domain either used generalized models applicable to all events or focused on specific, limited event types. Our proposal leverages a fine-grained event modelization method, allowing direct use of generalized models on a fine-grained event re-encoding. This re-encoding technique transforms events into graph representations of their associated nodes and temporal alignment. Experimentation with the T-IMDB dataset demonstrated the potential efficiency of our method.

Sapphire lasers with a high repetition rate, high pulse energy, and extremely short pulses are highly sought after in various applications.  Achieving stable Kerr-lens mode-locking in these lasers can be challenging, particularly due to their large spot size and high average power. This difficulty stems from the inherent dynamics between diffraction and saturation, which must be closely examined to establish stable locking.  By delving into the spatial and temporal evolution of beam propagation, it becomes clear that stable saturation occurs when the beam converging towards the mirror produces an expanded spot larger than the saturating region, while fast decay from the mirror occurs before the beam has traversed the entire length of the resonator.  Notably, in addition to standard considerations such as power, bandwidth, and pump intensity, higher pump intensity does not necessarily lead to stable locking, and spatial beam characteristics are as crucial as temporal ones in ensuring stable Kerr-lens mode-locking in these lasers.

Trend forecasting is a critical function with a multitude of applications across industries, including agriculture, where accurate predictions of key indices like corn prices can significantly impact a farmer's decision-making. The advent of Federated Learning (FL) presents an opportunity to improve forecasting quality while upholding data owner confidentiality. However, FL's efficacy in this context is hindered by the slow convergence of models, particularly for nonlinear regression tasks. This paper proposes a novel FL approach, Fed-AR, designed to overcome these challenges through the use of asynchronous, decentralized training utilizing PyTorch and optimized for resource-limited settings and nonlinear regression tasks. Fed-AR achieves this by leveraging a local gradient approximation method, which prioritizes updating parameters on devices with sufficient computational resources, thus accelerating model training and enhancing overall performance. Fed-AR's effectiveness is demonstrated on real-world datasets, including corn price data from the Farm Bureau, yielding impressive results.

To optimize the efficiency of thin silicon layers, which are often used in heterojunction solar cells, we investigated the absorption properties of thin films with 3D photonic band gap back reflectors compared to texturized, flat, and polished surfaces. Our simulations confirmed that thin films with 3D photonic band gap back reflectors exhibit higher average and integrated absorption rates than texturized, flat, and polished surfaces, with a maximum observed absorption rate of 99.5%. As the layer thickness decreases from 1000 nm, absorption rates either increase or maintain a high value below 1% under certain conditions, which were identified through numerical analysis. The improved absorption in thinner films is most pronounced in the lower frequency range. The overall structure of the solar cell, including the p-layer thickness, spacing between p and n layers, and design parameters of the 3D photonic band gap, influences absorption patterns and overall solar cell performance. The findings suggest that 3D photonic band gap back reflectors can enhance the performance of thin films, which could be a valuable strategy for improving efficient light absorption in the lower spectral range of thin-layer solar cells, which often experience reduced light absorption due to its longer wavelength.

We establish a primary set of equations that outlines the behavior of the principal branch of the iterated exponential function and provides a convergent series expansion for this function in terms of base $e$. Additionally, the set of equations and the series expansion hold for arbitrary bases and provide an exact and series expansion for the iterated exponential function. This formulation holds for arbitrary bases and provides an asymptotic expansion for large values of the iteration index. We demonstrate that the derived equations and series hold for arbitrary complex bases and provide an asymptotic expansion for large values of the iteration index for the function. This formulation is extended to the multi-valued function $e_{\!~f}\left(z\right)$. We derive an asymptotic expansion for the function $e_{\!~f}\left(z\right)$. This formulation is applied to study the behavior of the function $e_{\!~f}\left(z\right)$.

In this research, high dimensional expansions from covering are introduced, offering new approaches to asymptotic theory. It is particularly demonstrated that these expansions can rectify a long-standing issue regarding the finite sample convergence speed of nonparametric estimators in high dimensions, specifically jackknife estimators in high dimensional scenarios. The proposed high dimensional expansions are applied in various contexts, such as high dimensional discrete models and high dimensional random graphs, often occurring in conjunction with high dimensional expansions in high dimensional expansions. The methods employed rely heavily on the principles of empirical processes and weak convergence, frequently expressed through the use of Strassen coupling.

Researchers investigated the magnetic properties of the GdInO3 single crystal, focusing on its quasi two-dimensional honeycomb structure composed of Gd3+ ions. Experimental results, including magnetization curves and heat capacity analysis, were compared to theoretical predictions from a classical spin model. It was observed that the magnetic interactions are influenced by both in-plane and interplane magnetic exchanges, resulting in a compensation temperature where ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic components balance out. A second-order magnetic phase transition to a easily reoriented three-dimensional commensurate antiferromagnetic structure occurs upon cooling below the compensation point, and this phase transitions to a more complex antiferromagnetic structure upon further cooling. A comprehensive study of the magnetic properties, including the effects of temperature and field, was performed and compared to theoretical models.

Predicting connections in large networks, such as those representing scientific relationships or social interactions, is an important task with numerous real-world applications. The complexity of this task lies in its scope and the limitations of available data. While advanced machine learning models excel at predicting connections in specific contexts, they often fail to adapt to new situations effectively. In an effort to overcome these limitations, researchers have been exploring the use of transfer learning, which allows models trained on one type of network to predict connections in another type. Current approaches, however, rely heavily on the size and characteristics of the network from which a model is trained. While this strategy can lead to some success, it is not without its limitations. In an attempt to develop a more universal method that is not dependent on network size or properties, we have created Social Structure Node Embedding, an algorithm that uses graph representations to translate network structures into a common space. This translation enables an embedded node to predict connections with other nodes across various networks. The algorithm outperforms existing methods in predicting connections in multiple networks and outperforms comparable models in predicting connections in a specific network. The algorithm achieves this success while being relatively efficient and using a small number of variables. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of SSNE in multiple contexts, including networks of different sizes and properties. All-optical atomic sensors hold great promise for maritime situations due to their capacity to process signal information and serve as sensors of geometry and fluid dynamics. A novel, advanced technology allows for the fabrication of sensors featuring a laser-trapped atomic vapor and an optically sensitive cavity. The vapor chamber, formed by etching, has a precise, narrow U-shape with sub-mm dimensions and a well-defined geometric shape. The atoms within the cavity possess a well-defined central velocity, resulting in an anisotropic distribution that restricts their movement to two specific directions. The integration of additional laser beams, specifically the repump and pumping lasers, plays a crucial role in creating the vapor by etching and maintaining the atoms within the cavity in a state of excitation. The fabricated cavity then senses the geometric shape and properties of the surrounding fluid through an anisotropic distribution of fluid flow. The properties of the vapor chamber can then be further adjusted by sealing one end of the cavity, confining the vapor and enhancing the selectivity of the sensor by closing the open end. The resulting device is then used to sense a target object's presence by detecting a shift in the sensor's properties. The device can then be further developed and used to demonstrate the feasibility of sensing fluid dynamics.

We evaluate the performance of various nonlinear disruption power models for identifying signal disturbances in dual-polarization optical communication systems using Fourier transform-based SPIN methods. Nonlinear disruption power, which can be accurately predicted or measured, defines the power level at which distortion-infused signals begin and affect the original transmitted signals. These models will be instrumental in determining the optimal transmission parameters, allowing operators to gauge the effectiveness of spatial modes and optimize transmission efficiency. We present a unified framework containing five nonlinear disruption power models, which have the potential to be applied to diverse 4D formats transmitters, where each model varies according to the transmitter configuration. Our analysis highlights the advantages and limitations of each model and provides a comprehensive comparison of their accuracy. Furthermore, this work proposes a method to accurately estimate non-linear disruption power for hybrid polarization formats, expanding the potential applications.

Recent advances in fire research have highlighted the need for quick and accurate wildfire prediction to minimize devastating effects. Current methods, relying on single or combined infrared and visible channel imagery, struggle to optimize overall performance. Our new framework addresses this challenge by leveraging the full capabilities of multi-spectral images through a sophisticated fusion technique incorporating multi-spectral training of a Generative Adversarial Network. By harnessing the potential of multi-spectral images, our approach offers enhanced visual representations of wildfires, prioritizing features identified by human observers as crucial for effective outcomes. Our proposed technique facilitates improved human ATD model collaboration by integrating domain expertise and boosting visual quality through a refined understanding of important features. Evaluations demonstrate that multi-spectral images produced by our method surpass the performance of existing fusion and multi-spectral image comparison methods.

Early detection of depression through analysis of individuals' social media behavior
holds significant potential for both acute and predictive diagnosis. However, its
successful implementation requires thorough research into current practices, their
results, and the possibilities of open-source tools for categorizing depression. In
this study, a large dataset of 472,611 social media posts was collected from
community platforms such as Reddit, which was annotated and split into training
and testing sets. Various feature engineering and machine learning techniques were
evaluated to identify indicators of depression, and a comparative analysis was
conducting to determine which approach produced the best results. The experiments
conducted indicated that using word frequencies resulted in the highest accuracy
rate among the features examined, reaching 75% for binary depression classification
and 68% for multi-class. These findings demonstrate that depression can be
identified from social media posts, highlighting its potential for both research
contributions and contributions to understanding mental health through informal
online dialogue.

Multi-compartment models have been effectively used to analyze infectious disease spread and study vaccination effects, but their structure can be overly restrictive. This research introduces a random compartment model, which dynamically changes its structure in response to disease progression. The model incorporates a non-deterministic law of mass conservation, allowing for probabilistic partitioning of the population into distinct compartments. The article provides theoretical calculations for the probabilities of different compartment configurations and introduces a novel criterion for identifying the most likely configuration. The model was tested using real data on COVID-19 outbreaks in two German cities, Hamburg and Heidelberg. Fitting of the model parameters enabled accurate prediction of future infection rates, confirming that probabilistic modeling can be a valuable tool in understanding complex epidemiological processes.

In our study, we investigated how the interaction between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole vibrations affects each other in nuclei. This coupling causes a particular excitation energy, known as a "tunneling gap," where the vibration transfer occurs, and we used it to understand the strength of the interaction. Our approach involved calculating the vibration spectra in two ways: with the interaction taken into account (including the tunneling gap) and without it (a more traditional method). The strength of the interaction and the associated tunneling gap have significant implications for our understanding of the dynamics of nuclear motion, and we found that this interaction has a substantial impact on the movement of matter within the nucleus. Its effects are most noticeable at the shell gaps in nuclei and are associated with the significant displacement of matter that occurs there. This interaction was found to affect a wide range of nuclei in a consistent manner and provided new insights into the movement of matter within nuclei.

A mathematical model describing the dynamic interaction between a solid object and a surface featuring stick-slip characteristics and static friction is investigated. This model is subject to a force control system, and its behavior under certain parameters is examined, particularly how it adapts in response to changes in the coefficient of static friction and the force applied, ultimately converging to a velocity of zero.

In the context of reinforcement learning, our approach addresses the issue of excessively volatile estimated action values by developing a maximum mean discrepancy based on the Bellman equation. Through under-exploration in dynamic and static settings with tabular Markov decision processes, our method effectively limits the variance of the estimated action value, while remaining close to its optimal value. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that a more stringent boundary can be achieved with our method and provide a better bound compared to the traditional target network approach.

In recent times, significant breakthroughs have been achieved in training large, complex models for recommender systems, with advancements still ongoing. Nevertheless, researchers continue to grapple with understanding user behavior and the intent behind their actions. Currently, user intent models often rely on user behavior data that has been aggregated, making it difficult to capture intent in real-time as users interact with the system. To address this challenge, a new framework called Hidden User Intent Framework has been developed to help determine a user's intent at each interaction. Key features of this approach include its ability to learn the user's intent for every next action, incorporate theoretical knowledge of probability and psychology, and adapt to diverse user behaviors, all without requiring prior segmentation. The framework's effectiveness was demonstrated on actual user data from a video-on-demand service, revealing surprising patterns of intent that were not previously known, and was found to outperform existing user intent models on various evaluation metrics.

The unfolding of a meromorphic Fuchs equation transforms its singularities into algebraic curves described by a specific polynomial equation.
The paper presents a transformation that results in the unfolding of a particular type of equation, known as the double confluent Heun equation, into a form that yields a polynomial G with degree two or less when the equation's parameter is substituted into it.
The article shows that using a specific type of transformation, the obtained equation can be simplified into a particular form called the generalized Heun equation.
The analysis reveals that this equation has four distinct solutions, each of which is expressed as a combination of two special functions: a Heun one and a Weierstrass $\wp$.
The study further examines the connection between the solutions of the new equation and its zeros, showing a pattern that contributes to the understanding of the equation's nature and providing a basis for representing the solutions graphically.

The covariance matrix estimation in multi-group data, where each group has a smaller sample size than the total sample size, is a common issue. This phenomenon is called group-wise heterogeneity. In such cases, combining sub-matrices from different groups may lead to inaccurate results due to differences in variance levels. This, in turn, affects the performance of subsequent tasks, such as multi-group genome-wide association studies, which are important for identifying disease-related genes. To address this problem, researchers have developed methods to estimate a single, unified covariance matrix for multiple groups. However, existing literature on this topic is fragmented, with few studies providing a unified theoretical understanding. This work aims to fill this gap by establishing novel theoretical foundations, including novel necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving perfectly positive semi-definite estimates. Additionally, this research introduces novel necessary conditions for the minimal number of required group-specific adjustments to positive semi-definite matrices, which helps to minimize additional computations. Furthermore, this work provides a unified theoretical understanding of existing methods, identifying which techniques can solve this problem under certain conditions. Finally, this research includes empirical demonstrations of the implications of these findings.

A crucial topological mapping that retains its essential features, despite lacking symmetry, is presented. This mapping connects the entire symmetric shape to every asymmetric part. The key concept here is interconnectivity, meaning a shape A is linked to B if every part of A touches either a part of B or the environment surrounding both. The topological mapping, based on this interconnectivity, can be constructed without resorting to the outdated yet still widely accepted Pearson's separation axes method, which heavily relies on symmetry. The proposed mapping is applicable across different geometric domains and is equally relevant to higher-dimensional spaces. The discussion also explores its broader implications on understanding geometry in general.

We present a novel observable, $\mathcal{R}_{LF}$, which assesses the ratio of non-diagonal to diagonal leptonic $b\to s$ transitions, to investigate possible non-standard interactions. This observable is particularly suited to being computed with perturbative QCD corrections and precise leptonic decay measurements. The observable's main contribution comes from the vector currents of the hadronic current, making it more effective in detecting tensor and vector Z' and $W'$ signals. Furthermore, we discuss its accessibility in various $b\to s$ processes, including semileptonic decays of $B$ mesons, $B$ decays to lepton pairs and $P$-wave final states.

This research explores nature-inspired algorithms to manage multi-channel systems with several agents via simple, decentralized communication network.  A novel decentralized controller is proposed, which can adjust the internal states of agents autonomously yet lead the multi-channel system to converge to a stable equilibrium.  A critical condition for the proposed decentralized controller's efficacy is demonstrated with theoretical analysis, and its state-regulation capability is shown to be independent of the network's connectivity structure.  Furthermore, the connectivity-independent design of the proposed decentralized controller renders it adaptable to dynamic changes in the network, allowing it to effectively regulate the system's internal states under both complete and non-complete network graph configurations.  A comparative study examines the proposed decentralized controller against a centralized approach, highlighting its practical potential in governing large-scale systems through their division into smaller, controllable modules.  Furthermore, the scalability of the proposed decentralized controller is illustrated by its successful application in governing a large-scale ocean surface water system via a modular design of the controller.

The global pandemic, COVID-19, has led to widespread infections and fatalities worldwide.  As the disease spreads, it is essential to maintain social distancing measures to minimize the risk of infection.  However, movement restrictions have resulted in significant mental health deterioration, particularly isolation and lack of human interaction.  To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed AI-based interventions to monitor mental health in real-time, enabling more informed policy decisions. This study focuses on building a binary classification model for COVID-19 two-phase prediction, which aims to categorize individuals according to their current disease status as "positive" or "negative", and also whether they should be isolated as part of the second-phase prediction, which is labeled as "isolate" or "not_isolate". By leveraging BERT's capabilities for text-based information analysis within medical notes, this model outperforms alternative proposals in two-phase COVID-19 prediction tasks.

This paper presents a comprehensive overview of networking research, focusing
on key topics typically studied by graduate students. It provides an in-depth
analysis of important issues, introduces foundational concepts, and shares
valuable insights gained from experienced researchers. The presentation is
carefully structured to facilitate understanding, and it covers a broad range
of critical networking research areas, ensuring a well-rounded outlook for
upcoming professionals in the field.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics has been broadened in this work to encompass various timeframes of change. We draw on the conceptual framework of 'durations', defining them as the lengths of specific periods - past, recent and future - where environmental and ecological conditions persist. To a large extent, the theoretical models for eco-evolutionary dynamics have been focused on the dynamics themselves, neglecting 'duration-dependent' effects that influence eco-evolutionary development. This work aims to bridge this gap by considering the ecological and evolutionary changes that occur over different durations - from the rapid changes that occur within days to the slower changes that occur over centuries. We explore a range of duration-dependent models that have not been developed within the traditional framework of eco-evolutionary theory. These models are further expanded by introducing novel regulatory mechanisms - frequency dependence, non-linearity and memory - which expand the range of possible eco-evolutionary outcomes. This work provides a comprehensive review of eco-evolutionary dynamics across different durations and introduces new models that have not been explored within the traditional framework of theory and modeling.

Despite considerable interest in understanding how speech-based self-supervised learning models are trained, the role of adversarial examples in this process remains poorly defined. Adversarial examples are specific inputs designed to manipulate model predictions, but their influence on self-supervised learning models is not well established. Previous studies of SSL models assumed these examples have no impact or pass tests only due to chance, yet some models demonstrated a mild response to adversarial examples. Since SSL models learn patterns in large datasets, it's possible that these examples could also convey task-relevant information, as seen with human vision. To investigate this, we developed a method to characterise the antagonistic sensitivity of models, using a specific criterion to measure how much information about the training data remains in adversarial examples. Results showed that this information can vary significantly between models, even those trained with the same data, highlighting a role for task-relevant information in SSL model training. To confirm this, we discovered common patterns in adversarial examples that differentiated models trained on similar data. Our findings reveal a new perspective on SSL model training, suggesting these models are particularly adept at learning both beneficial and detrimental information.

This study offers a thorough examination of the consequences of centralization in the context of cryptocurrency trading. It provides an in-depth review of Blockchain-powered Distributed Exchanges (BDX), innovative platforms that aim to bring cryptocurrency trading closer to a decentralized model through a unique, groundbreaking approach. The research then assesses the economic implications of BDX on network resilience, focusing on a key aspect - the transaction fee. The analysis is conducted through a comprehensive theoretical framework, taking into account both strategic and non-strategic behavior. The findings are presented in a series of theorems, offering practical guidelines on BDX functioning. The research then evaluates BDX performance using numerical simulations, considering a market with multiple cryptocurrencies and a large number of traders. The results reveal the effects of various market and trader interactions on BDX performance. This comprehensive study serves as a valuable resource for BDX operators, providing practical insights on maintaining and operating BDX in an efficient manner.

The integration of causal analytics into real-world scenarios often involves dealing with missing data. This data omission issue is frequently complicated by uncertainty surrounding the data's availability, which needs to be addressed. This problem's neglect is often measured using the E-value, which quantifies the uncertainty associated with drawing conclusions due to unanalyzed data. This study aims to develop a framework for performing sensitivity analyses by utilising E-value metrics and type I/II error rate simulation. The proposed approach will be evaluated through an empirical analysis conducted on known causal relationships between a confounding variable M, intermediate outcome T, and the main outcome of interest T*. The results from this study indicate that Bayesian sensitivity analysis is a viable solution for evaluating the impact of unanalyzed data using classical hypotheses testing principles.

The study of the quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q[\mathbb{A}_1]$ generates an algebra homomorphism with its twisted generator $x^{-1}$ and the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetry. This paper presents an exhaustive compilation of the series expansion of $\mathbb{C}_q[\mathbb{A}_1]$. The symmetric and antisymmetric properties of the coefficients of $x^{-mj}$ for $0 \leq m \leq 1$ and $0 < j \leq \infty$ are established. This work further clarifies the properties of the primary fields of $\mathbb{C}_q[\mathbb{A}_1]$ and its relation with the Verma modules $V_{q,m}$. The potential dangers of an Internet of Vehicles (IoV) data infrastructure, driven by the proliferation of intelligent transport systems and connected devices, are becoming increasingly concerning due to the exposure of sensitive information. With the advent of blockchain technology as a public ledger system, protecting IoV data and preventing data breaches becomes more feasible. However, the integration of blockchain technology into IoV data systems poses significant performance impacts and presents a complex framework for information dissemination. To overcome these hurdles, the integration of blockchain technology into an IoV data infrastructure presents an opportunity for secure and efficient data protection, while maintaining the confidentiality of sensitive information. A possible solution is the implementation of a blockchain-enabled federated learning framework in IoV systems, facilitated by the integration of distributed ledgers and distributed machine learning models. This implementation enables the secure and collaborative training of machine learning models for IoV safety applications, while allowing for the secure integration of edge computing nodes into the blockchain-enabled framework. A blockchain-enabled federated learning framework, with the integration of secure and distributed data sources, can facilitate the training of reliable machine learning models for IoV safety applications, while promoting data security and user privacy through the exposure of anonymized data to multiple entities for decentralized learning processes. This system promotes decentralized training and testing of machine learning models for IoV applications, while ensuring secure and robust data protection and privacy preservation.

The LHC experiment measured the production of D0 and D+ mesons without prompt formation in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV. The findings are presented for integrated and differential characteristics, including transverse momentum, rapidity, and forward rapidity regions. The data are compared with theoretical predictions from Monte Carlo models, providing insights into non-prompt D-mesoon jet fragmentation. Additionally, direct D-meson production is assessed on an event-by-event basis, examining beauty and charm alignment. The alignment between charm and beauty quarks was found to be essentially independent of transverse momentum. The observed transverse momentum spectrum of direct D mesons matched Monte Carlo model predictions, with differential cross-sections consistent with previous studies at varying collision energies.

Our access to extremely cold quantum bits, or qubits, is crucial for the study of quantum computing and quantum communication. Presently, there are only a few specialized platforms capable of operating at such low temperatures as 10 millikelvin. Although custom-built quantum processors now exist at this temperature range, they can only be maintained for a short period using helium-3 cooling. In response, a 50-watt helium-3 refrigerator has been integrated into our quantum computing development lab at the University of Chicago's Research Accelerator, providing continuous millikelvin cooling for up to 5 days straight. This setup includes an adjustable dilution refrigerator and three distinct levels of strain-free sample mounts to accommodate a wide array of materials for quantum computing across semiconductor, superconductor, spin, and Ising model systems. Isolated platforms, or "islands," are also available for supporting larger-scale qubit arrays, which can be used to create vast quantum networks connecting distant locations. Moreover, a 6-inch by 2-inch "quantum stage" with a built-in piezoelectric material provides a highly adjustable platform for studying complex quantum systems. This highly versatile research platform not only aids us in our pursuit of quantum computing but also paves the way for groundbreaking research in the field.

The increasing adoption of Python in industry is evident, and this is largely due to its diverse range of applications, from data analysis and machine learning to real-time system development. However, the fact that Python is widely used doesn't necessarily mean it's always used correctly; in fact, there are many potential errors to watch out for, especially when developing cryptographic applications.  This research sets out to document and study common usage mistakes made when implementing cryptographic functionality using Python, and, through an analysis of publicly accessible GitHub code, reveals a considerable number of such mistakes present in open-source code.  By identifying and exemplifying these common errors, this research aims to contribute valuable knowledge that can aid in improving the existing Crypto module as well as educating developers to enhance the security of their Python-based cryptographic applications.

In diverse urban environments, audio recordings represent a crucial component, encompassing a wide range of applications from language dialects to music, with traditional recording methods relying on digital devices being superseded by mobile processing. The resurgence of interest in Automatic Speech Recognition and audio content analysis is attributed to the proliferation of mobile devices capable of recording and processing digital media. The effectiveness of current approaches, however, is often validated using standardized evaluation datasets compiled from digital archives. These datasets may not accurately reflect real-world conditions, given the variability and richness of noise, dialects, and cultural influences present in diverse multi-lingual settings. We propose an innovative solution, WORTH, to this challenge. WORTH is a system designed to automatically annotate speech dialects in real-time by leveraging polling-based user engagement. We demonstrate the feasibility of WORTH using a multi-modal annotation interface for online user engagement, showcasing its performance using in-car user recordings compiled into an unstructured dataset. The WORTH source code is publicly accessible through the https://github.com/asharv/worth repository.

This research introduces a novel neural network architecture, the NuSPAN network, specifically designed for deconvolving sparse signals. The signal sparsity in this case isn't uniform, characterized by a known pattern, like impulses in seismic data. The conventional approach to addressing this type of sparsity involves using total variation regularization, but we've found a more efficient method by using a learning-based network that can accurately interpret the sparsity pattern. The result is a more precise estimate with fewer distortions in the reconstructed data. The formal proof of the network's ability to identify the optimal solution despite its complex, nonconvex nature involves functionals with sparsity-promoting and total variation regularization terms. We've performed theoretical analyses on the network's ability to recover the sparse model and proved that it's capable of finding the exact solution under ideal conditions. This framework can be applied to various synthetic and real-world datasets with uniform and nonuniform sparsity patterns, and we've found that the NuSPAN framework consistently outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and stability. The potential applications of this innovation are vast and could be adapted to other areas with sparsity-related challenges.

This study investigates semigroups composed of composition operators acting on specific types of function spaces, specifically those related to BMOA, and explores the connection between these semigroups and integral operators. Initially, we establish a definition for a class of composition operators whose semigroups satisfy certain locality and boundedness conditions, and demonstrate that such semigroups are essentially equivalent to a class of integral operators possessing similar boundedness properties. Subsequently, we identify sufficient criteria for a composition operator to be part of a semigroup, and in turn, we identify sufficient conditions for the boundedness of a semigroup composed of composition operators, both within and across various function spaces. Ultimately, we apply these findings to a specific geometrically constrained set, and prove a relevant boundedness statement in the context of BMOA spaces.

A previously developed operator amalgamation technique is used to prove the presence of correlations in Haagerup's model through infinite-dimensional correlations derived from wavefunction overlaps and their associated bounds. This technique is further adapted to yield exact correlations with a linear dependence on system length. The findings for Haagerup's model are compared with existing results from a different approach. The proposed method can also be applied to general models with a Q-lattice structure, yielding a linear dependence of correlations on system length. The study concludes by addressing potential limitations of Haagerup's model as a real-world scattering system.

Automatically assigning part-of-speech labels to large collections of past texts is an essential yet complex task within linguistic research. Historically, linguistic models created for modern languages have performed well in similar tasks for other languages, yet their effectiveness varies when applied to individual languages and collections. Given that past collections often lack annotated data when compared to today's resources, reliable part-of-speech labeling for these collections poses a significant challenge. This study proposes a solution to this problem, employing a predictive model based on neural networks called a set-valued forecasting model that can accurately assign part-of-speech labels to unseen collections. This approach is validated by testing its effectiveness on six datasets from different languages and collections, including one language which has significant diachronic changes. The results demonstrate that the employed model accurately assigns part-of-speech labels for various datasets, with an average performance of 89.6% accuracy on unannotated data from one language and 75.2% on data with significant diachronic changes. Furthermore, the model's adaptability and reliability are shown to be consistent across different collections and languages.

This research paper explores a collection of new non-smooth integrability criteria, complementing the traditional smooth conditions previously outlined by Helmholtz and Lie. We establish a non-smooth analogue of Helmholtz's conditions using geometric methods and demonstrate that these conditions can be effectively expressed in both intrinsic and extrinsic forms. These findings provide a robust framework for validating local integrability of non-smooth vector fields. To illustrate the practical applications of these conditions, we apply them to vectors derived from one-forms with discrete or right-discontinuous variations. Moreover, we use a Lie algebra framework to extend our results to a broader class of special linear algebraic groups and their associated non-smooth subgroups, while also providing a detailed case study focusing on the rotational SO(2) group under various scenarios.

An increasing number of expectations are being raised for modern cities. 
For example, a city's administration may expect its green spaces to suffice
for both pets and people's needs. This type of informal expectation needs to be
reinterpreted to match the city management's official standards, akin to a law.
Our approach involves using an automated tool to translate these ambiguous
expectations into precise specifications, suitable for evaluation with the city's current facilities.
Our method includes a system for labeling data related to cities and a model based on the ALCOQ logic framework that accepts natural language inputs.
This paper offers comprehensive guidance on utilizing the tool, accompanied by a demonstration of its application to a scenario involving Petal Park in Birkbeck, the UK.
Additionally, the tool's source code has been made available for public access on GitHub.

We suggest using the concealed inverses protocol (CIP) to correct errors in quantum computations performed with binary codes. By employing CIP within a superconducting quantum circuit, it's feasible to utilize a conventional stabilizer code for error correction. CIP's ability to correct $n-k$ errors in $q$ bits can correct $n$ errors in a $q$-ary code. This makes CIP a versatile tool that, when employed, eliminates the constraint of limited qubit resources in error correction. Furthermore, by utilizing CIP, it's possible to utilize standard stabilizer codes for correcting a variety of errors, including those caused by spontaneous double bit flips, even in systems where qubit decay is prevalent. This approach also offers an alternative method for correcting errors that traditional stabilizer codes cannot, including errors that occur in the most stable qubits, providing a potential solution to the constraint of limited qubit resources in error rates.

In a regular category, a preorder can be represented using a subobject classifier through its correspondence to subobjects that satisfy specific conditions, in turn forming an equivalence relationship. The preorder's order can be utilized to define subobjects that satisfy certain properties, which in turn give rise to an equivalence relationship within the category. When employing the subobject classifier in a regular category, it is possible to develop a unique and distinct representation of the preorder that is formed through the application of a certain subobject-dependent function, in turn yielding an equivalence relationship within the category. The characterization of the subobject-dependent function that results in an equivalence relationship is particularly straightforward in categories with binary products and coproducts, as it necessitates the satisfaction of certain conditions.

Marine environments that experience severe weather events influence future coastal flooding and need to be studied by statisticians to better understand and predict these occurrences. In this research, a multivariate spatial model is developed to analyze co-occurring extreme weather events, focusing specifically on the relationships between storm surges, wind, and atmospheric pressure. To identify significant correlations between weather phenomena, both in terms of pressure patterns and geographical location, a multivariate peak over distribution model is employed. Our findings show that there are noticeable correlations between storm surges and wind speed. Additionally, it is discovered that there are local differences in extreme weather events, consistent with historical precipitation patterns in the region.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic confusions and insignificant, noisy texts. In response, we introduce a technique that refines VT-CLIP by increasing the feature vectors' visual direction through application of attention mechanisms. This refinement generates new, high-quality text embeddings via a learning objective that prioritizes visual congruence. Case studies demonstrate that visual guidance can effectively rectify inaccurate text associations. Furthermore, our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art VT-CLIP method in zero-shot and few-shot classification tasks, with comparable results to large-scale fine-tuned models.

Real-world applications involving matrix systems are often compromised by varying degrees of noise within a broad spectrum - a fact evident from the numerous practical issues that arise. The existing time-delay compensation method is capable of stabilizing unstable systems but comes with the limitation of only addressing problems where the desired output's stability does not depend on input signals. This means it's not suitable for models where vocabulary and non-vocabulary words intersect, such as speech recognition systems dealing with background noise, that require a combination of normalization and regression. Furthermore, previous research-based approaches can only tackle specific types of noise and are not adaptable to various noisy matrix systems. In our present study, an operator-switching method is introduced to address a wide range of noisy matrix problems effectively. Specifically, an operator-switching recurrent network architecture is developed to tackle rigorous systems where each step's convergence relies on the previous output. In real-world scenarios, such systems rarely exist and therefore, an operator-switching dilated convolutional model is developed to address problems where a large dilation rate is preferred. The models integrate a universal dilated convolutional network, capable of handling different noisy matrix problems. The models' effectiveness are tested on a range of noisy super-resolution tasks including speech, image, and video applications.

Our spectral sequence theory, applicable to any finite Bredon category $\mathcal{A}$ equipped with a stratum $R$, generalizes Cech homotopy theory for spectra with module structures. By extending the theory to spectrally graded categories, we analyze the spectrum theory in more complex situations. Key conclusions about quaternionic spectra and extended Bredon categories are established, particularly in relation to categories representing sheaf-like structures.

Given a k-rational local ring R with a characteristic different from 2, we define a compact Hilbert Polynomial for k-rational quasi-regular local rings. This definition is derived from the connection established by Fujita, Nadel, and Ein, Laza, Huamberto using Navier's formula, which shows that the polynomial's degree equals 1 for an F-stable local ring. This result builds upon previous findings by Alonso-Torres, Naranjo, and Sbarra. Furthermore, we found an alternative proof employing Ramino's formula, alongside an example of a non-F-stable local ring possessing a compact Hilbert Polynomial.

In the context of image data, including both radiology and pathology, 
machine learning model outcomes and annotation data necessitate standardized encoding.
The DICOM standard, widely adopted in radiology, provides a suitable framework for standardizing encoding, including support for binary and categorical data, large images, and complex metadata.
The highdicom package leverages the dicom2num and dicomnum2 Python libraries to convert data between the DICOM standard and base 64 numbers, enabling analysis of DICOM data.
The package offers functions for encoding model results and annotation data, as well as reconstructing original DICOM files from the encoded data.
The example use cases involve a breast cancer diagnosis project and a H&E anatomic region segmentation project, showcasing the utility of the DICOM standard and highdicom package for multiple application domains.
The package aims to enhance data portability, facilitate interdomain comparison, and provide a unified analysis environment for cross-domain research, all while promoting data sharing and reproducibility. 
The highdicom package can be used within Jupyter Notebooks for interactive work, and in standalone Python scripts for batch operations.
The package provides analysis functions for image level machine learning model outcomes, including predictions, confidence, and confidence standard deviation, as well as global image-level annotations.
The highdicom package includes functions for standardizing encoding of large and small images, as well as binary and multi-class categorical data.
