These galaxies, which experience few or no significant mergers, tend to lose gas through accretion at too slow a pace to build massive, luminous stars. As a result, their mass in gas diminishes over time, often never reaching the levels necessary to fuel the star formation associated with massive, luminous galaxies. Characteristics of these galaxies, including their star formation and gas reserves, have been predicted at various stages of their evolution. We analyze the impact of binding fermionic quasiparticles to local bosonic excitations using BCS theory. Our study reveals that merging these quasiparticles results in an unconventional reduction due to the increased influence of the bosonic field when compared to the standard BCS model. Notably, the rate of this unconventional reduction not only surpasses the conventional reduction but also does so at a rate proportional to the square of the coupling between bosons and electrons. This distinctive reduction is associated with the increased influence of the bosonic field on each merged fermionic quasiparticle. In the context of ultracold atoms trapped in optical lattices this reduction can be observed as a decrease in the discrete eigenvalue of the single-site Hubbard Hamiltonian. Furthermore, the rate of this decrease can be calculated using Gorkov and Eliashberg's formalism. The reduced eigenvalue increases with the square of the U/N ratio, a trend linked to the increased influence of the bosonic field on each merged fermionic quasiparticle and displays an inverse proportionality to the phase space filling factor.

The Thompson's groups T, T~, and T** have known growth functions of $\Omega(\log\log n)$, $\Omega(\log n)$, and $\Omega(n)$ respectively. Extending this work, the growth rates of their generalized versions, denoted by $d_i^s n \cong T^S$, as well as the braided Thompson groups $T_{\mathcal{B}}^1$, $T^1_{\mathcal{B}\bullet}$, and $T^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{B}}$, are found to be $\Omega(\log\log n)$, $\Omega(\log n)$, and $\Omega(n)$ respectively.

Although the RAG framework effectively retrieves relevant sentences based on input queries, its current implementation lacks the ability to directly respond to questions following the input. To address this limitation, we've developed an enhanced RAG framework that incorporates a question-answering component, allowing it to engage in in-depth question-and-answer conversations by retrieving and integrating relevant context from the retrieved sentences. This refined model, which builds upon the DPR seeker in conjunction with the RAG framework, outperforms existing models on question answering tasks and demonstrates exceptional robustness in handling questions that contain ambiguous language or substandard grammar and semantics.

Despite being a widely used task for ground truth, data quality issues plague summarization tasks. We investigate the effect of worker qualifications on summarization tasks and Unexpected Inclusionity, a measure of summarization performance. We qualify workers based on their performance in smaller tasks to ensure high-quality human annotation. With these guidelines, only 3.7% of workers are considered proficient. We discover that worker qualifications impact the correlation between worker IDs and summary quality, with top performers exhibiting better summary quality and reduced variability. Moreover, workers with qualifications demonstrate reduced agreement among themselves, indicating less consistency problems. In addition to leveraging qualifications to improve data quality, we also explore the notion of qualifications as a form of signal manipulation, allowing qualifications to be used in a targeted manner rather than randomly assigned. Ultimately, we demonstrate that qualified workers produce higher-quality summaries compared to randomly assigned ones.

Our proposed TS2-Net is a retrieval framework for long-text queries and compressed text clips. It simplifies complex queries by breaking them down into distinct tokens, shifting their timeframes, and reordering them. TS2-Net leverages a customized transformer to focus on both overall query representation and inter-token relationships, enhancing its general recall ability. Notably, TS2-Net achieves an outstanding mAP of 72.2% on the Nuclien dataset without relying on pre-trained models, making it the first retrieval system for multi-sentence data without this prior training. On the more challenging Nuclien+ dataset, TS2-Net reaches a high mAP of 64.1, significantly outperforming existing state-of-the-art solutions by substantial margins.

Beyond standard two Higgs doublet models in an extended new physics landscape, 
a notable possibility exists where new physics affects flavor only without influencing collider observables.
We explore this option with a single scalar particle at the heart of a top-quark-based taste-altering neutral current at the LHC, a scenario that allows simulation of a signal resembling a standard EW TC in the same final state but with a top quark-based TC pattern in the kinematics of the top quark and jets.
The research shows that with sufficient LHC data and appropriate analysis, it's feasible to distinguish taste-altering neutral currents from standard TCs with confidence levels exceeding 5 sigma, regardless of the parameter space of the model.

This study introduces a new class of random graphs called directed hybrid random graphs, which integrate preferential connection links with uniform linkage mechanisms. The existing methods of studying link prediction or graph dynamics in complex networks, such as percolation and random walks, are limited to specific types of connections. To address this issue, we propose a basic model of directed hybrid random graphs that incorporates both preferential connection links and uniform linkage mechanisms. We then establish fundamental yet general criteria for the mean field theory of this model, making it applicable to various specific cases, such as the Erdos-Renyi random graph, the directed scale-free transport model, the ferromagnetic Ising model, and the voter model. By assuming the existence of the mean field solution, we demonstrate that the model's behavior can be effectively described using a single equation, providing a unified framework for understanding various random graphs.

The expansion of wireless communication systems has significant implications for the environment, particularly when it comes to the pollution of the wireless spectrum. If unmanaged, this pollution can lead to service disruptions, even though strategies exist to mitigate such disturbances. One potential solution involves detecting these disruptions through the analysis of received signal strength. This study explores the use of wireless disturbance detection as a multi-label problem where multiple disturbance types can co-occur. Existing work in this area has been focused on detecting a single type of disturbance. We propose the use of a convolutional neural network to address the challenge of distinguishing between various disturbance labels. The performance of our proposed approach was tested using measurements collected from a diverse range of devices and scenarios, and the results demonstrate the feasibility of identifying multiple disturbance types.

This study explores the behavior of particles influenced by cosmic string spacetime and an additional space-time displacement for a particle's position, utilizing the Klein-Gordon equation. In this investigation, solutions that incorporate a vector potential with a cosmological constant are considered. The work provides complete energy spectra for particles in both electric and magnetic modes, accounting for any relationships between charge, rotation, and energy. The research also examines how rotation and charge interact to influence the particle's energy levels. The study shows that as charge increases, rotational effects decrease, and vice versa. Additionally, the study finds that for particles with zero rotational motion, an increase in charge leads to a decrease in energy, and vice versa.

Deeply virtual photon scattering, encompassing both Compton scattering and DVCS trigging the photon, is a crucial area of study for the development of hadron physics at current and future lepton-disk lab facilities. Traditional measurements have focused on the differential cross-section, transverse single-spin asymmetry, and the twofold cross-section transverse, while considering a coordinate system with the virtual photon's momentum driving the process. Within this framework, the longitudinal proton polarization asymmetry becomes noticeable when the integrand reduces to terms dependent only on the twist-2 contributions from generalized parton distributions. Researchers have suggested considering proton recoil polarization as a distinct observable in the study of DVCS. This novel observable, detectable with high precision using a 11 GeV electron beam at JLab and potentially at a future EuroGamma facility with an energy of 12 GeV, is particularly sensitive to higher-twist effects and reflections at the yield, independent of the virtual photon's momentum transfer. Using the PVDIS route, researchers can link this observable directly to parton distribution functions, making it extremely versatile and applicable across a broad range of experiments, applicable across a broad range of Q^2. This novel observable can serve as a reference point within the study of DVCS, assesses novel high-twist effects, and reflects the detailed structure of the proton at the level of partonic constituents. A longstanding aspiration of artificial intelligence is to create a system that surpasses human intelligence across all areas of knowledge. Achieving this goal requires a fundamental shift in the way AI is conceived and engineered. The possibility of creating such a system has been debated for centuries, with perspectives ranging from theoretical limitations to practical feasibility. In this paper, we present a novel, theoretically sound approach to AI and evaluate its potential for creating a superintelligence. By merging established psychological and neurological theories with modern artificial neural networks, our approach focuses on replicating the human brain's intricate structure and function. The proposed framework aims to leverage recent advancements in machine learning as efficiently as humans learn from experience. The paper also explores potential engineering methodologies for creating such a system using existing technologies and discusses theoretical implications for realizing enhanced AI.

Our study focuses on highly interacting cold bosons interacting with a variety of light and sound in a specially designed grid. This structure is designed to create unique interactions between neighboring units and break the spin parity, a phenomenon similar to those found in solid structures but with the spin-orbit interaction weakened. This research examines the changes in the optical lattice's characteristics at low temperatures, particularly in the case where the lattice undergoes a superfluid phase transition. This investigation reveals two possible phases: one with uniform superfluid phase and another with the superfluid phase split into two. The critical point for this phase transition is evaluated, as well as its dependence on the parameters of the strong interactions, showing significant changes for various interaction strengths. This research finds that the critical point's location changes based on the parameters of the strong interactions, resulting in two possible critical points, one for each phase. This study demonstrates that the optical lattice's critical point can shift in a complex pattern, depending on the parameters of the strong interactions, with the shift occurring in a modulated way for certain interaction strengths and resulting in two possible critical points, one for each phase.

Research into the properties of complex networks has gained momentum across various disciplines due to its widespread applications. The topological characteristics of these networks can be effectively characterized through graph theory, enabling comparison with real-world networks and artificial or generated ones. The connection between graphs and finite abelian groups offers a valuable framework for understanding graph symmetries, with benefits for problem-solving and algorithm optimization. This correspondence, however, only accounts for a network's symmetrical attributes, neglecting its structural properties. Here, a group-theoretic approach is proposed to address graph degeneracy – a crucial aspect of a network's topological structure. The distance to perfect adjacency of a graph can be measured by its distance to perfect irreducibility, correlating with the highest rank of its graph's symmetry group. This relationship is foundational for a broader theory connecting graphs to finite abelian groups, allowing for the exploration of a hierarchy of graphs within a standardised framework. The introduced hierarchy offers a comprehensive view of graph properties, with applications in multiple network-related areas. The theory and resulting graph hierarchy were effectively demonstrated through examination of well-known network types, such as scale-free networks, random networks and quasi-crystalline networks.

Our investigation explores the AdS/CFT correspondence in two and one spatial dimensions. We focus on two different scenarios: first, two-dimensional AdS$_3$ spacetime, for which we examine D3-branes in four-dimensional type IIA supergravity with a non-compact WZW gauge sector. In the second scenario, one-dimensional AdS$_1$ spacetime, we investigate the duality with conformal QFT in zero-dimensional systems. Unlike conventional approaches, our analysis is based on a simplified type IIA solution, where the non-trivial Ramond-Ramond field resolves the symmetry, resulting in distinct AdS dual representations. We demonstrate that the first scenario yields novel, previously unreported solutions, encompassing both BTZ-NS and BLLee-Zhang solutions, originating from non-linear symmetries. The second scenario reveals a novel solution that expands the existing duality framework, associating it with the dual conformal QFT. In both scenarios, we address potential generalizations and discuss the impact on the dual theory, also examining the role of non-compact gauge sectors in these reduced-dimensional systems.

A Gaussian Process regression model's effectiveness heavily relies on the choice of kernel, which determines the expected similarity between any two points. In this study, we explore kernels based on fundamental mathematical expressions like addition, multiplication, and exponentiation, and their respective derivatives. These basic kernels can be combined in various ways to accommodate distinct input features. We establish a framework for constructing such kernels and present two specific examples – one involving a kernel based on the difference between power and exponential functions, and another based on the derivative of the geometric mean of inputs, the square root of inputs, and linear combinations of these. Notably, the latter satisfies a crucial condition called positive-definiteness. We rigorously prove this and other fundamental properties, and empirically demonstrate the performance of these kernels on datasets covering a wide range of domains. Interestingly, our findings show that the geometric mean kernel offers better prediction performance compared to established GP kernels like the squared-exponential and linear kernels on various datasets.

Future muon colliders are expected to be highly susceptible to beam-induced backgrounds. Consequently, effective strategies are needed to manage these effects and reduce noise in collider detectors. This article examines potential strategies for managing beam-induced backgrounds in muon colliders. A key strategy involves optimizing particle intake patterns to minimize background noise in detector components. By modifying the way particles are collected and integrating advanced signal processing techniques, significant reductions in noise can be achieved. To illustrate the benefits of these strategies, demonstrations using simplified detector models are presented, highlighting the advantages of tailored particle intake and advanced signal processing in optimizing detector performance.

Introducing Spartan, a novel neural sparsity technique that utilizes a dynamic sparsifying function along with a random permutation matrix drawn from the cache of a matrix. This method leverages the permutation matrix, akin to Kornai et al.'s approach (2015), but replaces their non-differentiable heuristic with a differentiable transport-based approach. This novel strategy allows for easy integration into current neural frameworks, making it highly adaptable and applicable in a wide range of applications. The optimality of the permutation matrix is achieved through the maximization of the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and interestingly, its order resembles that of the eigenvalues of a given matrix. Furthermore, the eigenvalue order can be reversibly manipulated using the permutation matrix. The two differentiable components of the Spartan model are exploited in a series of experiments, and it is observed that its interplay with regularizers significantly boosts model sparsity, surpassing previous techniques like Kornai et al. (2015), Thulasidasan et al. (2020), and ENAS (Zhang et al., 2017).

According to the Bloch theorem, gapped systems in periodic media exhibit dispersionless bands within the Brillouin zone. However, when particles are not at absolute zero, lacuna-free phases may not be sustainable due to the possibility of surmounting any obstacle to spin flipping within the momentum space. Researchers have recently discovered a specific case where this happens - a one-dimensional system comprising one-spatial and two-sublattice Mott insulators. In our study, we explore an opposite scenario and report the initial documentation of a non-interacting, frameless phase in three-dimensional space - a case where spin-1 bosons, featuring a non-zero total momentum, cannot be converted into each other through weak interactions. This discovery was possible through the computational simulation of bosonic fermion mixtures that exhibit topological order. As a result, this finding offers an unprecedented opportunity to study a non-interacting, robust global phase that may be achievable in current Bose fluid experiments.

Previous studies suggest that bad code smells are linked to performance issues, but what about their impact on developers? Do developers even notice these smells, and do they think they are a problem? A recent study gathered feedback from crowd-sourced platforms, listening in on developers' conversations, and collected 375 statements expressing opinions about code smells. Among the key findings, most developers consider code smells to be unpleasant, and many view them as serious issues, often causing frustration and annoyance. Notably, some developers also associate code smells with boredom and fatigue, indicating that serious problems can arise from overlooked minor issues.

This paper investigates the resolution of variational inequalities featuring a nonconvex, time-varying graph and a time-dependent integral component. Specifically, it examines the movement of a particle subject to obstacles that change over time and have nonconvex shapes. The study first establishes that with certain restrictions on these obstacles, a unique path exists that satisfies the variational inequality. Next, it shows that even without these restrictions, a unique path exists that approximately satisfies the variational inequality, with the approximation error potentially unlimited but arbitrarily small.

We introduce a new Monte Carlo event generator, KKMCee, designed for creating events involving lepton and quark pairs in high-energy lepton collider environments. This tool integrates the matrix-element generator Polarsoft with the Monte Carlo generator KKMC, and includes features for polarisation preservation, especially in the study of polarised beams. KKMCee's performance in generating events, including efficiency, accuracy, and processing speed, is presented through a comparison with MadGraph5_aMC@NLO for different processes. In addition, we provide a detailed explanation of the implementation and interconversion methods between the two generators, and confirm KKMCee's reliability by studying polarisation in various processes while also ensuring equivalent efficiency in generating events compared to MadGraph5_aMC@NLO. This new event generator, KKMCee, is particularly suited for comprehensive studies of polarised beam collisions at future lepton colliders such as ILC, CLIC, and CEPC.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals is crucial for assessing cardiac health because changes in this interval can indicate cardiovascular problems such as heart disease.  However, identifying IBI from signals contaminated with noise and interferences poses a significant challenge.  To overcome this limitation, we have developed an innovative method using Tiramisu framework, which employs UNet for ECG signal denoising and subsequent IBI extraction.  Our approach begins with UNet-based Tiramisu framework to remove noise from the raw signal, followed by wavelet transform and thresholding to recover the IBI.  Notably, our method using UNet produces more accurate results with lower error rates compared to established techniques like wavelet transform and BASS.  The high accuracy of our approach is supported by the substantial reduction in error rates observed during testing on noisy datasets.  Furthermore, the visual comparison of reconstructed signal and IBIs using our method with known reference standards confirm its superiority over other techniques.

The singular value factorization of tensor values is valuable for analyzing multivariate data but is resource-intensive for large datasets. We've developed a stochastic algorithm for tensor singular value factorization (TSVf) and have based it on the matrix version using random projections. This approach reduces memory demands and allows us to select the number of passes (and thus compute speed) and accuracy (and thus approximate accuracy) adaptively. We choose the number of passes (t) based on projected matrix dimensions and approximate accuracy (ε) based on these projections. Our TSVf solution involves multiple iterations of random projections, matricization, singular value decomposition, and data selection. This algorithm can be used to compute projected tensor singular values and multiply the projected tensor-rectangular matrix. We demonstrate that our TSVf algorithm has linear computational complexity and logarithmic depth, making it scalable for distributed computing. We've also developed a stochastic algorithm to approximate multiply the projected tensor-rectangular matrix using a large number of processes, achieving high parallelism. We've evaluated our TSVf solution using datasets from climate studies and compared it to NumPy's version, showing that our solution matches numpy's accuracy while operating at the same speed or faster on smaller and medium-sized datasets.

Real-world networks often exhibit dynamic properties, necessitating the representation and analysis of changing graph structures. The goal of this research is to create a mathematical framework for embedding dynamic graphs in a stable Euclidean space. The proposed method extends a previous algorithm by Adams et al. to handle changes in graph topology over time, but initial experiments showed that it was not well-suited for direct application in this context. Therefore, a new approach based on Adams' work has been developed, combined with the edge embedding technique proposed by Dong et al. The result is a single algorithm capable of embedding a graph at any given time point without access to future information. The method achieves near-optimal metric distortion through a novel clustering approach that incorporates the Shotton star metric to maintain stability under topological shifts. The algorithm's performance was demonstrated by our team in experiments comparing various embedding techniques on dynamic social network data.

Theoretical research focusing on a $^3$H+4n system as an interesting resonance has gained attention, given its potential to meet the requirements for seven hydrogen isotopes. Utilizing the Faddeev equations within the framework of the Sectors formalism, we have calculated the amplitude of the $^7$H resonance emerging from the $^3$H+4n resonance's $1S$+ $3D$ states. Additionally, we have included an empirical correction for the $0^7S_1$ ground state, originating from the $^3$H+4n system's Coulomb displacement. Our findings suggest that the $0^7S_1$ ground state, rooted in the $1S$+ $3D$ configuration's non-strange component, provide the dominant contribution to this system. Calculations indicate a $0^7S_1$ resonance energy of approximately 4.04 MeV with a width of about 0.027 MeV. Our research supports the view of $^7$H's ground state as a $^3$H+4n resonance in the 1S+3D configuration, specifically offering key parameters such as resonance energy and width that align with experimental measurements within specified energy ranges.

Reiterating a query about a renowned unsolved problem in Riemannian geometry, Nirenberg inquired about the possibility of embedding strictly positively curved manifolds into other, positively curved manifolds of the same dimension. This question has been successfully addressed in certain lower dimensional cases, but the problem remains unresolved in higher dimensions. In this talk, we will present an alternative interpretation of Nirenberg's question, applied to the surface of a half sphere, aiming to embed its curved portion into another sphere of the same dimension, with specified curvature properties. Furthermore, we will demonstrate a counterintuitive finding – there is no universal bound to the curvature of embedded surfaces, which could potentially contain the half sphere's curved portion, if the curvature's sign is unrestricted.

A new class of neural network training objectives, known as Sinkhorn distances, has been introduced for supervised and semi-supervised learning. These objectives, derived from dynamical systems and optimal transport theory, have been tested on benchmark datasets for their robustness against adversarial attacks and their ability to improve semi-supervised models. In particular, semi-supervised learning frameworks have shown to be superior to other methods when the dataset is small, and this new approach surpasses a renowned method, the Sinkhorn Contrastive Diversity training. It's worth noting that ADC is linked to a GAN-like training process, but the new objective outperforms it as well.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, contact tracing programs were hastily established across the UK. In England specifically, two contact tracing programs were operational - the national program and eight regional programs. Each regional program varied in scope and efficiency, influencing their performance. We evaluated the impact of these variations using Bayesian analysis, considering factors such as the national program's infectious period, detection rate, and seizure rates. Notably, we found that regional programs with higher detection rates contributed significantly less to the overall tracing effort, whereas those with improved investigation rates could compensate for their effect. Conversely, national and efficient regional programs complemented each other to enhance the overall tracing effort.

The findings suggest that regional collaboration can be beneficial in contact tracing, particularly when investigation rates vary significantly. However, the results also indicate that regional programs should not be overly relied upon for reducing the infectious period. Instead, resources should be focused on enhancing the national program's efficiency, especially through enhanced investigations. Such findings provide valuable insights for informing public health policy and preparedness for potential future outbreaks.

The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance and urgency of establishing effective contact tracing programs. The rapid deployment of the national contact tracing program in England brought associated challenges, particularly in balancing resource limitations between tracing and investigation efforts. To address these challenges, regional collaboration was established, varying in scope and efficiency. A key question arose as to the influence of regional programs on the effectiveness of the national contact tracing program, prompting us to investigate.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides high precision data for this purpose. A detailed photometric study of the Melotte 72 star cluster has been carried out, employing precise filters to derive key cluster parameters. The cluster's location in the Milky Way, specifically in the second Galactic quadrant ($49.ion^{\circ}$), allows it to pass through the spiral arm. The Gaia DR2 survey offers precise distances for sources within the survey. The cluster's Gaia DR2 distance of $2.774^{+0.151}_{-0.099}$ kpc kpc aligns with other photometric and literature values. The determination of Melotte 72's fundamental parameters, including age, mass, and solar analogue status, are presented within this work. Employing various methods, the cluster's age and mass are found to be around $1.0^{+0.2}_{-0.3}$ Gyr and $(1439^{+283}_{-394}) \mathcal{M}_{\odg}$, respectively. Due to its proximity and high metallicity to the solar value ($0.080^{+0.015}_{-0.016}$, or $0.2 \mathcal{Z}_{\odg}$), Melotte 72 could potentially serve as a benchmark in stellar forensics research. Betti numbers represent key topological features that encapsulate complex data's intrinsic characteristics. In the context of Gaussian processes, the conditional covariance matrices are elliptical symmetric, resulting in Betti numbers that remain unchanged under linear transformations or projections. This invariance suggests performing geometric data analysis in the elliptic domain to retain meaningful topological information. However, practical applications often deal with sparse domains, which may not adequately represent the data-generating process. This work investigates the sparse domain's implications on Betti numbers, showing their potential discontinuity with respect to the mean field. To bridge this gap, a proposal is made to combine multiple journey samples into a topological data analysis framework, which can effectively characterize complex data. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, even with a limited number of samples.

In robotics, adjusting eye-in-hand cameras to navigate complex environments effectively is crucial, especially in tasks involving visual inspection. However, current methods are often time-consuming and require significant computational resources due to the need to generate 3D models or simulate camera poses. This research presents a novel approach that enables pose estimation for in-hand cameras based solely on an provided image and without requiring 3D modeling or simulation. This innovative method reduces the complexity and time required for training, while being portable on various hardware configurations. It is particularly beneficial for tasks such as object inspection and inspection-related tasks in diverse environments. Preliminary experiments demonstrate the method's superiority in terms of training efficiency and performance, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques in both metrics.

We focus on the problem of restricted reinforcement learning, where an agent aims to find an optimal policy for a markov decision process defined by a teacher. The limitations arise from two constraints: the agent must employ one of the teacher's predefined policies and the rewards it receives are calculated based on an unknown scaling factor. Our study involves investigating this learning problem with varying levels of information available. When the agent has access to a list of potential strategies from the teacher, we have created an efficient algorithm whose success rate approaches 1 - ε as the number of options grows for a fixed ε. If the agent can see the teacher's reward values during its learning process, we have devised an algorithm whose success rate approaches 1 - ε for a fixed number of states and actions, provided the number of strategies is sufficiently large. Our results indicate that the existing RL methods are insufficient to solve this problem due to the lack of access to the teacher's strategies. Additionally, we have found a lower bound for the number of strategies the teacher must employ to solve this problem, which supports the efficiency of our algorithms with minimal additional assumptions.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of the galaxy by studying a small percentage of the 100 billion stars within it, which may number over 400 billion. This article summarizes how the mission will work, what instruments it will use, and how it will contribute to understanding our galaxy. 

A critical element of the mission is creating an accurate 3D map of the galaxy's stars using observations from two small telescopes that scan the entire sky in tandem. This mission will offer numerous opportunities for educational outreach and global research collaborations due to its focus on the Milky Way, which is easily accessible from Earth. 

A comprehensive understanding of the galaxy's structure and composition may become possible with the data the mission will collect. This may include insights into how the galaxy formed, its composition, and movements. Additionally, the mission will help identify unrecorded binary stars and those in early stages of movement away from their original locations. 

GAIA's core scientific objectives include creating an accurate 3D map of the galaxy's stars, charting the galaxy's structure, and examining relationships between stars that offer clues to their classifications, compositions, and movements. 

Astronomers can use the data the mission will collect to study many aspects of the galaxy. This may include its general structure, star types, and motion using the data the mission will collect. 
Furthermore, the mission will help identify distant stars and those in early stages of movement away from the galaxy

Vertex divider structures serve a crucial purpose in graph theory by enabling the breakdown of a given graph into manageable tree-like components. The vertex divider structure's size directly impacts the graph's treewidth, which is why researchers aim to minimize it. The vertex divider structure's creation can be viewed as a parameterized problem, and recent findings aim to establish parameterized tractability. To achieve this, researchers typically compare the number of sets needed to cover the vertex divider structure. Unfortunately, most existing research findings suggest a polynomial parameterization hardness for specific parameters, including pathwidth and treedepth. This study presents a new parameterization, inspired by space constraints, to overcome these limitations. The proposed parameterization leads to the establishment of a new upper bound for the vertex divider structure's size, with explicit bounds for several graph parameters. The findings apply to multiple vertex separator parameters, offering a more general characterization. The results imply that pathwidth and treedepth, in particular, admit a polynomial parameterization for the vertex divider structure's size, with implications for $O(\alpha)$-approximation algorithms for specific NP-hard graph problems. The study also introduces a new parameterization, inspired by group treewidth and weak treewidth, for the vertex divider structure's size. The proposed parameterization offers a more general characterization of known research findings, with potential applications to the optimization of specific graph problems.

Network analysis with a traditional two-mode approach is insufficient for understanding its two distinct components, respondents and attributes. To overcome this limitation, a weighted directed grouping method has been developed. This new method captures how characteristics of respondents are perceived by attributes, making it a suitable statistical technique for directed two-mode networks. Our study discusses the directed grouping method's interpretations and identifies the necessary conditions for applying it in three types of networks: those derived from surveys, inferred from available data, and those based on assessments. Our investigation highlights the assumptions and requirements of the directed grouping approach.

A novel approach is proposed for validating the accuracy of physics-based neural networks, with a focus on those trained using experimental or simualted data. This method allows for an independent assessment of a network's accuracy on unseen data points, utilizing only its predictions and a few additional requirements. It does not rely on knowing the network's training process, unlike previous approaches. This proposed method is demonstrated on a network trained using datasets from the LHC, but it can also be applied to other fields that utilize physics-based neural networks. 

The key elements of this method are inspiration drawn from the principles of a posteriori verification, flexibility in application to various types of networks, and adaptability to various fields of use. 

A potential consequence of this approach is that it facilitates collaboration between physicists and engineers, with the latter being familiar with the concepts of a posteriori verification. 

The code to implement this method has been made public and can be accessed at the provided URL.

Epidemiological studies utilize diverse sources of data to understand the evolution and behavior of infectious diseases. During the 2020 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2, researchers incorporated environmental data into their studies, employing innovative methods of integrating global location-based tracking and atmospheric circulation patterns. This combination enabled researchers to leverage artificial intelligence and geostatistics to better comprehend the dynamics of the virus. Similar approaches will be necessary for managing and mitigating future outbreaks. However, they often rely on inaccurate or incomplete atmospheric circulation datasets, which are typically available on coarse grids. This results in substantial errors associated with modeling that can be misleading. To rectify this issue, we will demonstrate the use of neural networks to generate high-resolution atmospheric circulation patterns, which can effectively capture the characteristics of complex and dynamic weather patterns such as tropical cyclones.

A Majorana fermion, a proposed quantum entity, remains theoretically unverified and could hold the key to practical applications in the future. Various attempts to confirm the presence of Majorana states through tunneling spectroscopy have been reported, but alternative theories and factors such as tunneling conductance and local density of states are still unclear and may lead to false positives for the Majorana signature. To help distinguish the Majorana peak from other potential features in these scenarios, this study suggests a framework to understand and analyze the data. Our findings also highlight the impact of ohmic dissipation and a resistive environment on the emergence of zero-energy Majorana states. The outcomes indicate that if the Majorana peak were to coexist with other features at the same energy level, it would be distinguished by specific characteristics tied to tunneling length and resistance, but in cases of low tunneling, the dissipation might obscure the Majorana signature. In cases of high tunneling, the presence of a resistive environment would likely suppress the Majorana peak. This study proposes a framework for distinguishing the Majorana feature in edge-driven states that could be applied to future investigations.

Our investigation involved evaluating Linear Bandits, a type of contextual bandit problem, where each action corresponds to a vector representing its characteristics. A learner observes context $X_t$ at time $t$, and must then decide on the optimal action between a finite set $\mathcal{S}$. The objective is to maximize rewards by choosing the best action for the given context while utilizing a policy that anticipates future contexts. The ground truth action might not always exist within the available options $\mathcal{S}$, and we considered two distinct scenarios: (i) when the actions may not cover all context possibilities but still ensure that every context has a corresponding action within the available options (partially covered contexts), and (ii) when every context has a corresponding action within the available options (fully covered contexts). Our work particularly examines a scenario with a limited number of actions where each action's characteristics are distinct. The simulation revealed that the current methods for evaluating linear bandit algorithms are not effective in assessing linear bandit algorithms that operate within partially or fully covered contexts with unique features. By employing a random context generator, our investigation showed that the ground truth estimate of feature variance $\sigma^2_\theta$ significantly deviates from its actual value when the actions' characteristics are limited. Consequently, our analysis indicates that the current methods for evaluating linear bandit algorithms that operate within partially or fully covered contexts with unique features are unreliable and may result in inaccurate parameter estimates.
